root.title: AI Engineering
root.text:
AI engineering is what you do when the model is a given. Someone else trained it, you cannot see inside it, you cannot fully predict it, and you have to build something dependable on top of it anyway. That constraint is the entire discipline. Every practice in this topic exists because the most important component in the system is one you did not write and cannot debug in the usual way.

Start from what a language model actually is: a function that takes a string and returns a probability distribution over the next token, sampled repeatedly. Not a database, not a reasoner, not an agent. Everything a real product appears to do beyond that — remembering a conversation, citing a document, calling an API, sticking to a schema, refusing a bad request — is scaffolding built around that one primitive by an engineer. The model supplies fluency and pattern-completion. You supply the correctness.

That inversion is why AI engineering does not reduce to normal backend work. In ordinary software the same input produces the same output, failures throw, and correctness is proved by construction. Here the same input produces different output run to run, failures are fluent and confident rather than loud, and correctness is a statistical property you can only estimate by measurement. You cannot unit-test your way to confidence; you have to build a measurement apparatus and treat quality as something observed rather than guaranteed.

The rest follows from that. Context engineering exists because the prompt is the only channel through which the model can learn anything about your problem. Retrieval exists because that channel is finite and your knowledge is not. Agents exist because one forward pass cannot take actions in the world. Evaluation exists because nothing above can be verified any other way. Serving and cost exist because all of it runs on hardware someone pays for, and safety exists because an untrusted string reaching a system with tools is a live security boundary.

children.title: Foundation Models as Components
children.text:
Before you can engineer around a language model you have to be precise about what it is, because almost every bad intuition in this field comes from imagining a different object than the one you are actually calling. The model is not a knowledge base, not a reasoning engine, and not a process that persists between requests. It is a function from a sequence of tokens to a probability distribution over the next token, applied repeatedly, with a randomised choice at each step.

Everything in this section follows from taking that definition literally. If output is sampled from a distribution, identical inputs give different results, and determinism is something you buy rather than assume. If the input is a bounded sequence of tokens, then the context window is a hard physical budget and every design decision downstream is an allocation problem. If the function has no state, then memory, personality, and conversation are illusions reconstructed on every call by whoever writes the request.

The reason to settle this first is that it draws the line between the model's job and yours. The model supplies fluent, plausible continuation of patterns it has seen. It does not supply truth, freshness, arithmetic guarantees, schema compliance, or restraint. Those are engineering responsibilities, and mistaking them for model responsibilities is how teams end up trying to fix an architectural gap by rewording a prompt.

children.title: What a Language Model Computes
children.text:
A language model is trained on one task and one task only: given a sequence of tokens, predict the next one. Not answer the question, not tell the truth, not be helpful — predict what token plausibly comes next in text like this. Everything the model appears to do beyond that is an emergent side effect of doing that one task extremely well over an enormous corpus.

That single fact explains most behaviour you will observe in production. It explains fluency, because fluency is exactly what next-token prediction optimises. It explains hallucination, because a plausible-sounding continuation is precisely what the objective rewards, and the objective contains no term for whether the continuation is true. And it explains why the model is so sensitive to how a prompt is phrased: phrasing changes what kind of text this looks like, which changes what plausibly comes next.

It also explains the gap between the raw artefact and the product. A model that has only been pretrained will happily continue your question with three more questions, because that is what a list of questions looks like. Instruction tuning and preference training are additional stages that reshape the distribution toward answering rather than continuing. When you call an API you are calling the post-trained model, and the distance between those two things is the difference between a text predictor and an assistant.
children.deep_text:
Concretely: the model holds a vocabulary of perhaps a hundred thousand tokens, and a forward pass over a context produces a vector of logits, one per vocabulary entry. Softmax turns those into a probability distribution. One token is chosen, appended to the context, and the whole forward pass runs again. A five-hundred-token answer is five hundred sequential forward passes over a context that grows by one each time. That is the entire generation loop, and it is worth holding in mind because it also explains the cost and latency model: output tokens are serial and therefore slow and expensive, while input tokens are processed in parallel and therefore comparatively cheap.

What emerges from that objective is more surprising than the objective itself. To predict the next token well across a broad corpus, a model has to implicitly represent syntax, factual associations, code semantics, translation mappings, and something functionally resembling multi-step inference — not because anyone specified them, but because each of them reduces prediction loss on some slice of the data. This is why capability scales with data and parameters in a way that feels discontinuous: the mechanisms were being learned gradually, but they only become usable once they are accurate enough to chain together.

The base-versus-instructed distinction deserves care because it is where a lot of prompt superstition originates. A base model completes documents. Ask it a question and a very reasonable continuation is a FAQ list containing more questions. Post-training — supervised fine-tuning on demonstrations, then reinforcement learning from preference data — reshapes the output distribution so that the completion of a question is an answer, and so that certain classes of completion are strongly disfavoured. It does not add a knowledge store or a reasoning module. It changes which of the model's existing continuations are likely.

The common misconception is that the model looks things up. There is no retrieval step and no stored table of facts; there are weights that make certain continuations probable. A fact the model reproduces reliably is one that appeared often and consistently in training in a form the weights could compress. A fact it gets wrong is often one that appeared rarely, inconsistently, or in a form that collides with a stronger pattern. This is exactly why retrieval-augmented generation works: putting the fact in the context replaces a weak statistical recall with a strong local copying behaviour, which the model is far better at.

The practical consequence for an engineer is that you should stop asking whether the model knows something and start asking whether the correct continuation is the most probable one given the context you constructed. That reframing turns a hopeless question about the model's mind into a tractable question about your input, which is the only part of the system you control.

interview.question: If a model is only trained to predict the next token, why can it follow instructions at all?
interview.answer: Because instruction-following text exists in the training distribution and is reinforced afterwards. Pretraining makes an instruction-and-response pair a plausible document shape; supervised fine-tuning on curated demonstrations and then preference-based reinforcement learning shift probability mass so that the most likely continuation of an instruction is a compliant answer rather than, say, more instructions. The objective never changes from next-token prediction — what changes is which continuations the weights make probable.

interview.question: Why are output tokens usually priced several times higher than input tokens?
interview.answer: Input tokens are processed in a single parallel forward pass over the prompt, so the hardware is used efficiently. Output tokens are generated one at a time, each requiring its own forward pass over a context that keeps growing, so generation is serial and memory-bandwidth bound. You are paying for the sequential dependency, not just the token count, which is also why latency scales with output length far more steeply than with input length.

interview.question: A colleague says the model 'knows' your company's internal API because it answered a question about it correctly. How do you interpret that?
interview.answer: Cautiously, and with a test. Either that material was in the training data, or the answer was a plausible reconstruction from conventions that happened to be right. Neither gives you a reliability guarantee, and the second failure mode is invisible because a confident wrong answer looks identical to a confident right one. The correct engineering response is to put the API definition in the context via retrieval rather than to depend on recall you cannot audit or version.

children.title: Tokens and the Context Window
children.text:
The model does not see characters or words. Text is first cut into tokens — subword fragments produced by a compression scheme fitted to the training corpus — and it is tokens that get embedded, attended over, billed, and counted against limits. Common English words are usually one token; rare words, names, code punctuation, and non-Latin scripts fracture into several.

This is not a trivial implementation detail, because it is the unit in which everything is measured. Your bill is in tokens. Your latency is roughly proportional to tokens. Your context limit is in tokens. A rule of thumb of about four characters per token holds for ordinary English and breaks badly for JSON, minified code, or Hindi, where the same information can cost two or three times more. Estimating budget in words rather than tokens is how teams get surprised by both cost and truncation.

Tokenisation also explains a whole family of otherwise baffling failures. A model that writes flawless essays may miscount the letters in a word, because it never saw the letters — it saw one opaque token. Reversing a string, counting characters, and character-level arithmetic are hard for the same reason, and no amount of prompt rewording fixes them, because the information was destroyed before the model ran.

The context window is the hard cap on how many tokens one call may contain, input and output together. It is the model's entire observable universe for that call: instructions, retrieved documents, conversation history, tool definitions, tool results, and the answer all compete for one finite budget. That competition is the central resource-allocation problem of AI engineering, and large windows relieve it without abolishing it, because attention quality and cost both degrade well before the stated limit.
children.deep_text:
Tokenisers are usually byte-pair encoding or a close relative. Start with raw bytes, repeatedly find the most frequent adjacent pair in the corpus, and merge it into a new symbol, for some tens of thousands of merges. The result is a vocabulary where frequent sequences are single symbols and rare ones decompose. It is a compression scheme, fitted to a particular corpus, and its biases are that corpus's biases: English prose compresses beautifully, code compresses less well, and languages underrepresented in the corpus compress badly. When a Hindi or Thai sentence costs three times the tokens of its English translation, that is not a policy decision, it is the merge table.

Several practical consequences follow directly. Cost estimates must be computed with the actual tokeniser for the model you are calling, not approximated from word counts, and the discrepancy is worst exactly where your payloads are worst: deeply nested JSON, UUIDs, base64, and stack traces are all token-expensive relative to their apparent size. Trimming a verbose retrieval payload is frequently a larger cost win than switching to a cheaper model.

The context window deserves a more careful treatment than a number. Attention cost grows quadratically with sequence length in the naive formulation, and while production systems use optimisations that soften this, the economics still push against very long contexts. More importantly, usable attention is not uniform across the window. Empirically, models attend most reliably to the beginning and the end of a long context and least reliably to the middle — the lost-in-the-middle effect. A fact placed at position twelve thousand of a hundred-thousand-token context is present but may as well not be. This is why stuffing an entire corpus into a large window is not a substitute for retrieval: retrieval is not only about fitting, it is about placing the relevant material where attention actually lands.

There is also a compounding subtlety in conversational systems. Because the model is stateless, every turn resends the full history, so a twenty-turn conversation pays for turn one twenty times. Token spend grows quadratically with conversation length unless you actively manage it through summarisation, truncation, or windowing. Teams routinely discover this only when the bill arrives, because a short demo never exhibits it.

The correct mental model is a budget with competing claimants. System instructions, tool schemas, retrieved chunks, conversation history, and reserved output space all draw on one pool, and the reserved output space is the one people forget: if you allow the input to consume the entire window, generation truncates mid-sentence. Every serious system needs an explicit accounting of who gets how many tokens and what gets evicted first when the budget is exceeded — and that policy should be code, not an accident of string concatenation.

interview.question: Why can a model that writes excellent code fail to count the letters in a word?
interview.answer: Because it never sees letters. The word arrives as one or two opaque tokens, and the character composition is not recoverable from the embedding except insofar as the model memorised spellings as facts. Character-level tasks ask the model to inspect information that tokenisation discarded before the forward pass began, so the failure is architectural rather than a matter of insufficient prompting. The fix is to do character-level work in code, not in the model.

interview.question: Your token costs are growing much faster than your user count. What do you look at first?
interview.answer: Conversation length, because a stateless model resends the entire history every turn, making spend grow quadratically with turns rather than linearly. After that, the retrieval payload — how many chunks are attached and how large they are — and whether verbose serialisation formats are inflating token counts. Both are usually fixable with a history-management policy and tighter retrieval budgets, without changing models.

interview.question: If the context window is a million tokens, why still build retrieval?
interview.answer: Three reasons: cost, latency, and attention quality. You pay for every token you send and you wait for them to be processed, so filling a huge window on every request is expensive and slow. More importantly, attention is not uniform — material buried in the middle of a very long context is measurably less likely to be used than the same material placed deliberately. Retrieval is a relevance and positioning mechanism, not merely a way to fit within a limit.

children.title: Sampling and Non-Determinism
children.text:
At each generation step the model produces a probability distribution over the whole vocabulary, and something has to choose one token from it. That choice is sampling, and it is the reason the same prompt gives different answers on different calls. The variation is not a defect or an instability in the hardware — it is a deliberate design choice built into how these systems generate text.

Two parameters do most of the work. Temperature rescales the logits before the softmax: below one it sharpens the distribution toward the already-likely tokens, above one it flattens it toward the unlikely ones. Top-p, or nucleus sampling, truncates the distribution to the smallest set of tokens whose probability mass exceeds a threshold and renormalises, which cuts off the long tail of genuinely bad options while leaving the plausible ones in play. Setting temperature to zero gives greedy decoding — always take the most likely token — which is as close to deterministic as you can practically get.

Even then it is close rather than exact, and the reason matters. Floating-point arithmetic on GPUs is not associative, so batching, kernel selection, and hardware routing can change the last bits of a logit, and when two tokens are nearly tied that is enough to flip the choice. Because generation is autoregressive, one flipped token changes the context for every subsequent token, and the outputs diverge completely from that point on.

The engineering consequence is that reproducibility is not available as a guarantee, and any practice that assumes it — exact-match assertions, response caching keyed on output, a single manual test taken as evidence of correctness — is built on sand. You have to design for a distribution of outputs rather than a value, which is precisely why evaluation later needs statistical methods rather than a test suite.
children.deep_text:
It helps to see why sampling exists at all rather than treating it as an inconvenience. Greedy decoding, always taking the argmax, produces text that is measurably worse for open-ended generation: it is repetitive, it falls into loops, and it is bland, because the locally most probable token is frequently not part of the globally best continuation. Sampling from the distribution recovers the diversity that makes generated text read like text. The randomness is buying quality, not costing it — which is why the answer to flaky outputs is rarely to force temperature to zero everywhere.

The right way to set these parameters is by task, and the deciding question is whether the task has one correct answer or many acceptable ones. Extraction, classification, routing, schema-filling, and SQL generation have one target, and diversity is pure loss — run them near zero. Drafting, brainstorming, naming, and creative rewriting have a space of good answers, and near-zero temperature makes them dull and repetitive — run them around 0.7 to 1.0. Most production systems are a mixture and should therefore not have one global temperature setting, which is a surprisingly common mistake: a single config value applied to a whole application guarantees that half the calls are mistuned.

Top-p and temperature interact and are usually best adjusted one at a time. Temperature reshapes the entire distribution including the tail, so a high temperature can promote genuinely incoherent tokens; top-p removes the tail first and then samples, so it tends to give diversity with a floor on quality. A common production configuration is a moderate temperature with top-p around 0.9, and a common mistake is cranking both, which produces the incoherence people mistakenly attribute to the model being bad.

The determinism question has a subtler layer that catches teams in regulated settings. Even with temperature zero and a fixed seed where the provider offers one, exact reproducibility is not contractual: providers update models behind a version label, batch requests differently under load, and route across heterogeneous hardware. Non-associative floating point means a different batch composition can change a logit in the last bits, and a near-tie resolves the other way. Because each token conditions everything after it, that single flip cascades. So a system whose correctness argument depends on byte-identical outputs is already broken; what you can legitimately depend on is that the distribution of outputs satisfies a measurable property.

That reframing is the practical payoff of this unit. Instead of asserting that a call returns a specific string, you assert that a schema validates, that a required field is present, that a claim is grounded in a retrieved source, or that a scored quality metric stays above a threshold across a sample of runs. Instead of debugging from one bad output, you run the same input many times and look at the distribution, because a failure that occurs in one run out of ten is invisible to a single manual test and very visible to your users at scale.

interview.question: Why not just set temperature to zero everywhere and get deterministic behaviour?
interview.answer: Because greedy decoding degrades quality on open-ended tasks — it is repetitive, prone to loops, and bland, since the locally most probable token often is not part of the best overall continuation. Zero is right for extraction, classification, and structured output where there is a single correct answer, but wrong for drafting or ideation. And it does not actually buy determinism anyway, because non-associative floating-point arithmetic across varying batches and hardware can still flip near-tied tokens.

interview.question: A bug reproduces roughly one time in twenty. How do you approach it?
interview.answer: Treat it as a distribution rather than an event. Run the same input a few dozen times, capture every output, and characterise what distinguishes failures from successes — whether it is a specific branch, a truncation, a schema violation, or an ambiguity in the prompt that sampling occasionally resolves the wrong way. Then either constrain the output so the failure becomes impossible, lower temperature for that specific call, or add a validation-and-retry layer. Fixing it by re-reading a single failed transcript usually fixes nothing.

interview.question: What does temperature actually do to the logits, and how does that differ from top-p?
interview.answer: Temperature divides the logits before the softmax, so values below one sharpen the distribution toward already-likely tokens and values above one flatten it, including the tail. Top-p instead keeps the smallest set of tokens whose cumulative probability exceeds the threshold and renormalises, discarding the tail entirely before sampling. The practical difference is that temperature can promote genuinely bad tokens while top-p sets a floor on candidate quality, which is why combining a moderate temperature with top-p around 0.9 is a common and stable configuration.

children.title: Capabilities and Failure Modes
children.text:
Designing around a component means knowing its datasheet, and the most useful thing you can internalise about language models is which of their failures are fixable by better prompting and which are structural. Confusing the two wastes enormous amounts of engineering time.

Models are genuinely strong at transformation and pattern completion: rewriting, summarising, translating, extracting structure from prose, classifying, drafting code, and explaining things that are well represented in their training data. These are tasks where the answer is largely determined by the input in front of them, which aligns exactly with what next-token prediction optimises.

They are structurally weak wherever the answer is not determined by the input and cannot be recalled reliably from weights. Hallucination is the flagship case: the objective rewards plausible continuation, and it contains no term for truth, so a confidently fabricated citation is not a malfunction but the objective working as specified. Recency is another — weights are frozen at a training cutoff, so anything after it is unknown. Exact arithmetic on large numbers, precise character manipulation, and reliable counting are all weak for reasons traceable to tokenisation and to the absence of an algorithmic execution step.

The most dangerous category is the third: capabilities that appear reliable until they are not. Multi-step reasoning often works and then fails on a superficially similar problem. Self-assessment is largely unreliable, because a model's stated confidence is generated by the same process that generated the possibly-wrong answer, not by an independent check. The correct response to all of this is architectural rather than rhetorical — supply facts through retrieval, delegate arithmetic to a calculator, enforce structure with a validator, and verify claims against sources — rather than instructing the model not to be wrong.
children.deep_text:
Take hallucination seriously as a design constraint rather than a defect to be complained about, because the framing determines whether you build the right thing. The training objective assigns loss for improbable continuations, never for false ones. Asked for a citation supporting a claim, the model produces the shape of a citation — plausible authors, a plausible journal, a plausible year — because that is the highest-probability continuation, and nothing in the objective distinguishes a real reference from a well-formed fake. Post-training reduces the frequency by making hedging and refusal more probable in some contexts, but it cannot remove the underlying mechanism.

That mechanistic view immediately suggests the remedy, and it is not asking the model to be accurate. It is changing the task from recall to copying. If the source text is in the context, producing a correct citation becomes a copying operation, which models are extremely good at, rather than a recall operation, which they are unreliable at. This is the actual first-principles justification for retrieval-augmented generation, and it also explains why RAG fails when retrieval fails: with no relevant document in context, the model falls back to recall and hallucinates as before, only now with more confidence because the prompt implied sources were available.

Arithmetic follows the same logic. The model has no arithmetic unit; it has statistical associations over digit sequences, which is why small sums are usually right and large multiplications are usually wrong in a characteristic way — leading digits plausible, middle digits invented. Chain-of-thought prompting improves this measurably by decomposing one hard prediction into several easy ones, but improvement is not a guarantee, and any system where the number must be right should call a calculator. The general principle: if a deterministic tool exists for the subtask, the model's job is to decide to call it and to interpret the result, not to perform it.

Self-knowledge is the failure mode that most often defeats otherwise careful engineers. A model asked how confident it is generates a confidence statement using the same next-token machinery that generated the answer, so stated confidence correlates with the linguistic conventions of confident text far more than with correctness. Similarly, asked whether it used a particular document, it produces a plausible answer about its own processing, which it has no privileged access to. Verification has to be external: check the claim against the source, validate the structure against a schema, use a separate call with a different framing that does not see the first answer's reasoning.

Reasoning deserves an honest treatment rather than either dismissal or hype. Something functionally like multi-step inference clearly happens, and it improves substantially when the model is given room to work step by step, because each step becomes a shorter inferential leap conditioned on explicit intermediate state. But it is not algorithm execution: it degrades with problem length, it is sensitive to surface phrasing in ways a real algorithm would not be, and it can produce a fluent derivation with a wrong step in the middle and a confident conclusion. Newer reasoning-tuned models push the reliability boundary outward significantly, and it remains a boundary. The engineering posture that survives model upgrades is to treat reasoning as a capability with a measured success rate on your task, established by evaluation, rather than as a property the model either has or lacks.

interview.question: How would you reduce hallucination in a customer-facing assistant?
interview.answer: Change the task from recall to copying, then verify. Retrieve the relevant source material into context so producing a correct answer is a copying operation rather than a memory operation; require citations that point at retrieved chunks; validate after generation that cited spans actually exist in the retrieved text; and design an explicit path for the model to say it does not know when retrieval returns nothing relevant. Prompt instructions like 'do not make things up' help marginally and should never be the primary control.

interview.question: Why is asking the model for a confidence score a weak safeguard?
interview.answer: Because the confidence is generated by the same next-token process that produced the answer, with no independent verification step. It reflects the linguistic register of confident text rather than a calibrated probability of correctness, so a fabricated answer frequently comes with a high stated confidence. Useful signals have to come from outside the generation — agreement across independent samples, validation against a schema or source, or a separate grader that does not see the original reasoning.

interview.question: A product manager wants the assistant to compute pricing totals. What is your design?
interview.answer: The model parses the request and decides which computation is needed; a deterministic function performs the arithmetic; the model presents the result. Any design where the model produces the number itself will be wrong occasionally and confidently, and pricing is exactly the domain where an occasional confident error is unacceptable. This generalises: when a deterministic tool exists for a subtask, the model's role is routing and interpretation, never execution.

children.deep_text:
This section is deliberately placed before any practical technique because the techniques are unreadable without it, and worse, they get cargo-culted. Engineers who never internalise the token-and-sampling picture develop a folk model in which the system is an entity with intentions, and then they debug it by negotiating with it — adding please, adding emphasis, adding threats — instead of by changing the mechanics that actually determine the output.

The four parts move from the inside outward. First, what the model computes: the next-token objective, what emerges from it, and the crucial distinction between a base model and an instruction-tuned one, because the thing you call over an API is not the raw artefact produced by pretraining. Second, tokenisation and the context window: the unit of currency in every API call, the reason character-level tasks fail strangely, and why the context budget is finite in a way that shapes the entire architecture above it.

Third, sampling and non-determinism: temperature, top-p, why the same request twice gives two answers, and what that means for reproducibility, caching, and testing. This is the property that separates AI engineering from ordinary backend work more sharply than any other, and it is the reason evaluation later needs a whole section rather than a test file.

Fourth, the capability boundary: a direct treatment of what these systems reliably do, what they reliably do not, and what they do in a way that looks reliable until it is not. Hallucination, arithmetic, recency, and self-knowledge belong here, framed not as bugs to be scolded out of the model but as predictable consequences of the objective it was trained on.

Taken together, the section leaves you with a component datasheet: inputs, outputs, cost model, failure modes, and guarantees. Everything after this is systems design around a component whose datasheet you now know.

children.title: Context Engineering
children.text:
Because the model is stateless and has no access to your systems, the context window is the total set of things it can possibly know when it answers. Not the most important input — the only one. Every fact, every rule, every example, every piece of conversation history that influences an answer is there because an engineer put it there on that specific call.

That reframing is why the discipline is called context engineering rather than prompt writing. Prompt writing suggests finding the magic words. What you are actually doing is deciding, under a hard token budget, which information earns a place in a finite window, in what order, in what format, and what gets evicted when it does not fit. It is an allocation problem with a measurable objective, which makes it engineering rather than incantation.

The first-principles framing also tells you what should and should not work. Instructions work because they establish what kind of text this is, which shifts the distribution over continuations. Examples work better than descriptions for anything with implicit conventions, because the model infers a pattern more reliably than it follows an abstract rule. Position matters because attention is not uniform across the window. And politeness or emphasis mostly does not work, because it does not change any of those mechanics.

This section covers the four things you assemble on every call: the instructions that set the task, the demonstrations that pin down the format, the structural constraints that make output machine-readable, and the reconstructed conversation history that creates the illusion of memory.

children.title: Designing Instructions
children.text:
An instruction works by making one kind of continuation more probable than another. That is the whole mechanism, and holding it in mind separates the techniques that work from the folklore that does not. Telling the model it is a careful technical editor changes the distribution of text that plausibly follows, because text written by careful technical editors has recognisable properties. Telling it that this is very important changes almost nothing, because importance is not a property that predicts the next token.

From that mechanism, a few reliable principles follow. Be specific about the output you want rather than the mistakes you want avoided: negative instructions require the model to represent the forbidden thing in order to suppress it, and are systematically less effective than describing the target directly. State constraints as properties of the deliverable — length, audience, format, what to do when information is missing — because those are checkable and they map onto observable features of the text.

Position matters for a mechanical reason. Attention is strongest at the beginning and the end of the context, so instructions buried in the middle of a long assembled prompt are measurably weaker than the same instructions placed at either edge. In long-context systems the common and effective pattern is to state the task up front, insert the retrieved material, and then restate the critical constraints immediately before the model generates.

Finally, treat the system prompt as versioned code rather than a string someone edits in a dashboard. It is executable configuration: it determines behaviour, it regresses when changed, and a change to it deserves the same review and the same regression run as a change to a function that half your traffic passes through.
children.deep_text:
The single most common failure in instruction design is under-specification masquerading as clarity. An instruction like summarise this document is perfectly clear to a human and radically ambiguous to a model, because it does not determine length, audience, level of technicality, whether to preserve numbers, whether to editorialise, or what to do with material that does not fit. The model resolves each of those ambiguities by sampling from what is typical, which means the result varies run to run along every unspecified axis. When someone complains that outputs are inconsistent, the cause is usually that the prompt left a dozen degrees of freedom open and sampling is filling them in differently each time. Consistency is bought by removing degrees of freedom, not by asking for consistency.

Negative instructions deserve their own treatment because they fail in a specific and counterintuitive way. Do not mention pricing places the concept of pricing into the context, raising its salience, and the suppression has to overcome that. It often works, but it works less reliably than the positive form, and reliability is the whole point. The general rewrite is mechanical: for every prohibition, ask what the model should do instead, and state that. Do not guess becomes if the document does not contain the answer, reply exactly with INSUFFICIENT_CONTEXT — which has the further advantage of being machine-checkable, turning a vague behavioural hope into a testable assertion.

Role framing is genuinely effective but for a narrower reason than the folklore suggests. It does not grant expertise the model lacks. It selects a register and a set of conventions from the training distribution, which affects vocabulary, structure, level of hedging, and what the model considers relevant to mention. A prompt that says you are a security reviewer will surface threat-model considerations that the same question without the role would omit, not because the model became a reviewer but because reviewer-authored text mentions those things. This tells you when role framing helps — when the desired output has strong stylistic and topical conventions — and when it is noise, which is when the task is fully specified by its constraints.

Structural formatting of the prompt itself matters more than it looks. Long prompts with clearly delimited sections — a consistent heading convention, or XML-style tags around retrieved documents and user input — outperform the same content run together as prose, for two reasons. The delimiters give the model unambiguous boundaries about what is instruction versus data, which reduces the chance that content inside a document is interpreted as a directive. And they give you a reliable place to insert and evict material programmatically. That first reason is also a security property: the boundary between trusted instruction and untrusted input is the surface that prompt injection attacks, and a clear structural convention is the first line of defence, though never a sufficient one.

The discipline that ties this together is treating prompts as versioned artefacts under measurement. They belong in source control with the code that uses them, they get a version identifier that is logged with every request so a production output can be traced to the exact prompt that produced it, and any edit is validated against an evaluation set before it ships. The alternative — a prompt edited live in a console by whoever noticed a bad output most recently — produces a system whose behaviour nobody can explain and whose regressions nobody can detect, and it is depressingly common precisely because prompts feel like text rather than like code.

interview.question: Why do positive instructions generally outperform prohibitions?
interview.answer: A prohibition requires the model to represent the forbidden concept in order to suppress it, which raises that concept's salience in the context and makes the suppression a probabilistic contest rather than a specification. Describing the desired behaviour directly shifts probability toward it without that contest. The practical rewrite is to convert every prohibition into a required alternative, ideally one that is machine-checkable — replacing 'do not guess' with an exact sentinel string to emit when information is missing gives you both better compliance and a testable assertion.

interview.question: A prompt works in testing and behaves inconsistently in production. What are the likely causes?
interview.answer: Most often the prompt under-specifies dimensions that the test inputs happened not to exercise — length, tone, handling of missing fields, what to do with edge-case inputs — and sampling resolves them differently on real traffic. Second, real inputs are longer, so instructions that sat at the front of a short prompt are now buried mid-context where attention is weaker. Third, the accumulated conversation history in production changes the context in ways a single-turn test never reproduced. The fix is to specify the open dimensions, reposition or restate critical constraints near the end, and evaluate on sampled production inputs rather than curated ones.

interview.question: How should prompts be managed as a codebase grows?
interview.answer: As versioned code: stored in source control alongside the code that calls them, given identifiers that are logged with every request so any production output can be traced to the exact prompt version that produced it, and gated by an evaluation run before any change ships. Prompts are high-fan-in executable configuration — a single edit can change behaviour for every request that passes through it — so editing them live in a console without a regression check is equivalent to pushing unreviewed code straight to production.

children.title: Few-Shot and Demonstrations
children.text:
A demonstration teaches by showing the mapping rather than describing it. Instead of explaining in prose what a good extraction looks like, you include three worked examples of input and correct output, and let the model infer the pattern. This works because pattern completion is precisely what the model does best — continuing an established regularity is far more reliable than following an abstract rule.

The decisive question is whether the task has conventions that are easier to show than to state. Formatting, tone, edge-case handling, level of detail, and domain-specific labelling conventions are all things where a paragraph of description leaves ambiguity that two examples eliminate immediately. Conversely, if the task is fully determined by a clear instruction, examples add tokens and latency without adding information.

What surprises most engineers is how much the choice of examples matters, and in what way. The model picks up on everything present in them, including properties you did not intend to teach. If all your examples have short inputs, long inputs get treated as out-of-distribution. If all of them are positive cases, the model becomes reluctant to produce the negative label at all. If they are ordered with all of one class first, ordering effects skew the output distribution. Demonstrations are training data delivered at inference time, and they carry the same biases that training data carries.

The practical discipline that follows is to select examples that span the actual input distribution — including the hard cases, the ambiguous ones, and the ones where the correct answer is to decline — rather than the clean cases that read nicely in a document. Examples that only show success teach a model that success is the only option.
children.deep_text:
The mechanism is worth being precise about, because it dissolves a persistent confusion. In-context learning does not update any weights. Nothing is learned in the training sense and nothing persists past the request. What happens is that the examples establish a strong local pattern in the context, and the highest-probability continuation of an established pattern is more of that pattern. This is why the effect is so sensitive to surface form: consistent delimiters, consistent field ordering, and consistent phrasing across examples strengthen the pattern, while inconsistency weakens it. Two examples formatted slightly differently from each other teach the model that format is not important, which is precisely the opposite of the usual intent.

There is a well-documented and initially shocking result about what examples actually contribute. Replacing correct labels in demonstrations with random ones degrades performance far less than you would expect, which tells you that much of the benefit comes from establishing the shape of the task — the input format, the output space, the length, the register — rather than from teaching the correct mapping. That does not license using wrong labels; correctness still helps, particularly on harder tasks. What it tells you is where to invest attention: getting the format and the coverage of the output space right is worth more than agonising over a marginal case in one example.

Example selection has a static and a dynamic form, and the choice between them is a genuine architectural decision. Static few-shot puts a fixed set in the prompt, which is simple, cacheable, and cheap — a fixed prefix is exactly what provider-side prompt caching rewards. Dynamic few-shot retrieves the most similar labelled examples for each input, typically by embedding similarity, which measurably improves accuracy on heterogeneous tasks because the demonstrations are always near the current case. The cost is a retrieval step in the hot path, defeated caching, and a second system to maintain. The rule of thumb: use static when the input distribution is narrow, dynamic when it is broad and you already have a labelled pool.

Ordering is not a detail. Models exhibit recency bias, weighting the last example more heavily, and this produces measurable skew in classification tasks when examples are grouped by class. If the final three demonstrations are all approved, the model's prior shifts toward approved. The mitigations are straightforward once you know to look: interleave classes, keep the class balance in the demonstrations roughly matched to the balance you want in the output, and if you are being rigorous, measure sensitivity by shuffling the order across an evaluation run and observing how much the metric moves. Large movement means your prompt is fragile in a way that will bite when someone edits it.

Finally, weigh demonstrations against alternatives honestly. Every example costs tokens on every single call, which is real money and real latency at volume. If you have hundreds of labelled examples and the task is stable and narrow, fine-tuning moves that cost from inference time to training time and usually outperforms few-shot on the same data. If you have a handful of examples, a task that changes weekly, or a need to explain behaviour to a reviewer, few-shot is the right tool precisely because it is inspectable and editable in seconds. The decision is about the stability of the task and the volume of traffic, not about which technique is more sophisticated.

interview.question: Does few-shot prompting train the model?
interview.answer: No. No weights are updated and nothing persists after the request. The examples establish a pattern within the context window, and the model continues that pattern because pattern continuation is what next-token prediction rewards. This is why the effect vanishes on the next call unless the examples are resent, why formatting consistency across examples matters so much, and why the technique costs tokens on every request rather than once.

interview.question: Your classifier over-predicts one class. How might the demonstrations be responsible?
interview.answer: Class balance and ordering in the examples both bias the output distribution. If most demonstrations are of one class, or if the final examples before the input are all of one class, recency and prior effects push predictions that way. The checks are to balance classes in the demonstration set, interleave rather than group them, and measure how much the metric moves when the example order is shuffled — large sensitivity indicates a fragile prompt independent of this particular symptom.

interview.question: When would you choose fine-tuning over few-shot prompting?
interview.answer: When the task is stable, narrow, and high-volume, and you have hundreds or more labelled examples. Few-shot pays the token cost of every example on every call, so at scale it becomes a large recurring expense and a latency tax; fine-tuning moves that cost to a one-off training run and typically beats few-shot given the same data. Few-shot wins when the task changes frequently, when labelled data is scarce, or when you need behaviour to be inspectable and adjustable immediately.

children.title: Structured Output
children.text:
A model that returns prose is readable by a human. A model that returns validated JSON is callable from code. That difference is what turns a demo into a component you can put in a pipeline, and it is why structured output is a foundational technique rather than a formatting nicety.

The naive approach is to ask for JSON in the prompt and parse the result. This works most of the time and fails in a long tail of specific ways that are individually easy to dismiss and collectively fatal at scale: a preamble sentence before the object, the whole thing wrapped in a markdown code fence, a trailing comma, an unescaped quote inside a string, a truncated object because generation hit the token limit mid-structure. At a thousand requests a day, a one-percent parse failure is ten broken requests a day, and each of them surfaces as an exception in code that assumed it had data.

The robust approach removes the possibility rather than handling the symptom. Constrained decoding — offered by providers as structured output, JSON mode, or grammar-constrained generation — masks the token distribution at each step so that only tokens which keep the output valid under the schema are eligible. Invalid output is not caught after the fact; it becomes unreachable, because the tokens that would produce it are assigned zero probability.

Understanding that mechanism also tells you its limits. A schema guarantees shape, never meaning. Constrained decoding will happily produce a perfectly valid object with a fabricated identifier, a wrong enum choice, or a confidently invented date, because it only constrains the grammar of the output. Structural validity is a necessary precondition for a reliable system and never a sufficient one, so semantic validation against your own data remains your responsibility.
children.deep_text:
Constrained decoding is worth understanding mechanically because it explains both its power and its costs. The schema is compiled into a state machine over the token vocabulary. At each generation step the decoder computes which tokens could legally come next given the current position in that machine — after an opening brace, only a quote or whitespace; inside an enum field, only tokens that are prefixes of a permitted value — and sets the logits of every other token to negative infinity before sampling. Malformed output is therefore not unlikely, it is impossible. This is a categorically stronger guarantee than any prompt instruction, which only makes malformed output improbable.

The cost is that the constraint fights the model's natural distribution, and this shows up in two ways. First, quality can degrade when the schema forces the model into a shape at odds with how it would naturally express the answer — an extremely rigid schema on a task that needs nuance produces technically valid, semantically poor output. Second, and more subtly, when the model wants to express uncertainty and the schema has no field for it, the constraint forces a confident value. A schema with only a required answer string cannot represent I do not know, so the model must invent something. The fix is to design uncertainty into the schema explicitly: nullable fields, an explicit confidence enum, a required flag for insufficient evidence. This is one of the highest-leverage design moves in the whole topic and it is routinely skipped.

Truncation deserves specific attention because it is the most common structured-output failure in production and the least obvious to diagnose. If generation hits the max-token limit mid-object, you get a syntactically invalid fragment — and with constrained decoding you get a valid-prefix-of-valid-object, which can be worse because it may parse as something incomplete rather than failing loudly. The mitigations are to reserve output tokens explicitly in your context budget, to cap the length of unbounded fields in the schema itself, and to detect the finish reason from the API response rather than inferring success from a successful parse. A response that stopped for length should be treated as a failure regardless of whether the fragment happens to parse.

Schema design has its own principles that are largely transferable from API design, with one addition specific to this setting: the field names and descriptions are prompt content. The model reads them. A field named x with no description carries no signal, while a field named refund_eligible_reason with a description explaining the permitted rationales measurably improves the quality of what goes in it. Enum values should be words with meaning rather than opaque codes, because the model is far better at selecting among semantically distinct options than among arbitrary identifiers. Flat structures generally outperform deeply nested ones. And field order matters, because generation is sequential: a field generated earlier is available as context for the ones after it, so putting reasoning or evidence fields before the conclusion field gives the model room to work before it commits — which is chain-of-thought smuggled into the schema, and it works.

The last discipline is semantic validation, which no amount of structural constraint replaces. After parsing, check that identifiers exist in your database, that dates are in a plausible range, that quoted spans actually appear in the source documents you retrieved, that numbers are internally consistent. Decide explicitly what happens on failure: retry with the validation error appended to the context, which is often effective because the model can see precisely what it got wrong; fall back to a simpler prompt; or escalate. What you must not do is let a structurally valid, semantically wrong object flow downstream, because at that point it has become indistinguishable from correct data and will be trusted by everything that touches it.

interview.question: What does constrained decoding guarantee, and what does it not?
interview.answer: It guarantees the output conforms to the schema's grammar, because tokens that would break validity are masked to zero probability at each step, making malformed output unreachable rather than merely unlikely. It guarantees nothing about meaning: identifiers can be fabricated, enum choices can be wrong, dates can be invented. Structural validity is necessary but not sufficient, so semantic validation against real data remains a separate and mandatory step.

interview.question: Your extraction returns valid JSON with a plausible but fabricated value when the document lacks the field. Why, and how do you fix it?
interview.answer: Because the schema made the field required and offered no way to express absence, so the constraint forced a value and the model produced the most plausible one. The fix is in the schema, not the prompt: make the field nullable, or add an explicit not_found sentinel or an evidence field that must quote the supporting span. Designing an explicit representation for uncertainty is the single most effective structural change for this class of failure.

interview.question: How does field ordering in a schema affect output quality?
interview.answer: Generation is sequential, so fields produced earlier become context for fields produced later. Placing a reasoning or evidence field before the conclusion field lets the model work through the problem before committing to an answer, which is chain-of-thought expressed through the schema and measurably improves accuracy on non-trivial tasks. Putting the conclusion first forces the commitment before the reasoning exists, and any subsequent explanation is a rationalisation of an already-sampled answer.

children.title: Conversational Memory
children.text:
A chat interface strongly implies that the system remembers you. It does not. The model is stateless: each API call is independent, and the only reason turn five knows what happened in turn one is that your application resent turns one through four as part of the request. Conversation is a client-side illusion, reconstructed from scratch on every message.

This has an immediate and uncomfortable consequence for cost. If every turn resends the full history, token spend grows quadratically with conversation length — a fifty-turn conversation pays for the first turn fifty times. Latency grows with it, since the whole history must be processed on every request. Systems that feel fine in a five-turn demo become expensive and slow in a fifty-turn support session, and the failure is structural rather than a matter of optimisation.

Eventually the history exceeds the window and something has to give. The available strategies are a genuine trade-off rather than a ranking. Sliding windows keep the last N turns and drop the rest, which is cheap and predictable and silently loses early context — including, frequently, the thing the user said at the start that defines the entire task. Summarisation compresses old turns into a running précis, which preserves the gist at the cost of an extra model call and lossy detail. Retrieval over history treats past turns as a searchable corpus and pulls back only what is relevant, which scales best and adds a whole retrieval subsystem.

The right framing is that memory is a policy you design rather than a feature you enable. What must always survive, what can be compressed, what can be dropped, and what should be extracted into durable structured storage instead of living in the transcript at all — those are four different questions, and answering them separately produces much better systems than picking one strategy for everything.
children.deep_text:
Start with the quadratic cost, because it is the thing that most often turns a successful pilot into an unsustainable product. Turn one sends the system prompt plus one message. Turn two sends the system prompt plus three messages. Turn N sends the system prompt plus roughly 2N messages. Summing over a conversation gives a total token count proportional to N squared, and since output tokens are the expensive ones only at generation while input tokens dominate by sheer volume here, the input side ends up being the majority of spend in long-conversation products. The single most effective mitigation is provider-side prompt caching, which is worth designing for explicitly: caches key on a stable prefix, so putting your system prompt and tool definitions first and never mutating them mid-conversation can cut the cost of that repeated prefix dramatically. A system that injects a timestamp at the top of the prompt defeats caching entirely, which is a genuinely common and expensive mistake.

The sliding window's failure mode is worth stating precisely because it is silent, and silent failures are the ones that reach users. Users typically establish the task in the first message — I am migrating a Postgres database to a new schema, help me through it — and then ask short follow-ups. Twenty turns later the window has evicted that first message, and the model, now seeing only a series of narrow technical questions, answers the current one without the framing that made it meaningful. There is no error, no exception, no log line. The answers just get subtly less appropriate, and users describe it as the assistant getting worse over time, which is exactly what is happening and exactly what the design guarantees.

Summarisation trades a different set of problems. It costs an extra model call, which adds latency at the moment it triggers, and it is lossy in a way you do not control: the summariser decides what mattered, and it will sometimes drop the specific identifier, version number, or constraint that turns out to be load-bearing three turns later. Two mitigations help substantially. First, summarise incrementally rather than re-summarising the whole history each time, feeding the previous summary plus the newest turns forward, which bounds cost. Second, and more importantly, hold a separate never-summarised region for pinned facts — the user's stated goal, their environment, hard constraints, decisions already made. Compression errors compound across repeated summarisation, so anything that must survive should not be subject to compression in the first place.

Retrieval over history is the most scalable option and introduces the failure modes of the retrieval section applied to a conversation. Past turns are embedded and indexed, and each new message retrieves the semantically nearest ones. This handles arbitrarily long histories and surfaces a relevant exchange from two hundred turns ago, which neither other strategy can. Its weakness is temporal: conversations have a strong recency structure and a strong causal structure that pure semantic similarity ignores, so it can retrieve a superseded decision instead of the one that replaced it. Any serious implementation has to blend recency with similarity and, ideally, track supersession explicitly.

The most valuable distinction in this unit is between conversation history and durable memory, because conflating them is the root of many bad designs. History is the transcript of what was said. Durable memory is extracted structured state — the user prefers metric units, the account tier is enterprise, the deployment target is AWS — stored in an ordinary database, keyed to the user, and injected as a compact block on every relevant request. Facts belong in durable memory; only the transcript belongs in history. This makes the important information cheap, permanent, inspectable, editable, and deletable, which also happens to be what privacy regulation requires: a user asking you to forget a fact is trivially satisfiable when facts are rows and effectively impossible when they are diffused through a summarised transcript. Design for the extraction step early, because retrofitting it means reprocessing every conversation you have stored.

interview.question: Why does the cost of a chat application grow faster than the number of messages?
interview.answer: Because the model is stateless, every turn resends the entire prior history, so the tokens sent over an N-turn conversation grow roughly with N squared rather than linearly. A fifty-turn session pays for the opening message fifty times. Mitigations are history-management policies — windowing, summarisation, or retrieval — plus provider-side prompt caching, which requires a stable, unmutated prefix to be effective.

interview.question: Users report the assistant 'gets worse' late in long conversations. What is your first hypothesis?
interview.answer: That the history strategy has evicted or compressed the framing established in the opening turns. With a sliding window the initial task description is dropped outright; with summarisation a specific constraint or identifier gets compressed away. Either way there is no error, just answers that no longer reflect the original context. The fix is a pinned, never-evicted region holding the user's stated goal and hard constraints, separate from whatever compression applies to the rest of the transcript.

interview.question: How do you distinguish conversation history from memory, and why does it matter?
interview.answer: History is the raw transcript; memory is structured state extracted from it and stored in a real database — preferences, environment, decisions, entitlements. The distinction matters for cost, since a compact fact block is far cheaper than a transcript; for reliability, since a fact in a row cannot be summarised away; and for privacy, since deleting a fact is a row deletion when memory is structured and effectively impossible when the fact is diffused through compressed transcripts across many sessions.

children.deep_text:
The reason this section comes before retrieval, agents, and evaluation is that all three are special cases of it. Retrieval is context engineering where the material is selected at query time from a corpus. Agent design is context engineering across a loop, where each turn's context includes the accumulated results of previous actions. Evaluation measures whether your context assembly produces good outputs. If the assembly step is ad hoc string concatenation scattered through a codebase, none of the later disciplines can be applied cleanly, because there is no single place where the input to the model is decided.

The most valuable structural idea in this section is to treat context assembly as a first-class component with an explicit budget and an explicit eviction policy, rather than as an artefact of how the code happened to be written. In a mature system there is a function whose entire job is to take a request and produce the final token sequence, with a documented allocation: so many tokens for system instructions, so many for tool schemas, so many for retrieved material, so many for history, and a reserved floor for output. When the budget is exceeded, something must be dropped, and which thing gets dropped is a design decision that deserves to be written down and tested rather than discovered in production when a long conversation silently truncates the system prompt.

The four parts proceed from the static to the dynamic. Instruction design covers the persistent frame: role, task, constraints, and the ordering that survives long contexts. Few-shot demonstration covers teaching by example, when examples beat descriptions, and how the choice and ordering of examples changes behaviour more than most engineers expect. Structured output covers the transition from prose to data, which is what makes a model callable from ordinary code rather than merely readable by a human. And conversational memory covers the fact that a chat has no server-side state — the history is a string you rebuild, and how you compress it as it grows determines both quality and cost.

Throughout, hold on to the mechanism: you are shaping a probability distribution over continuations by controlling the text that precedes them. Every technique in this section either adds information the model needs, or makes the desired continuation more probable relative to its alternatives. Techniques that do neither are superstition, and the way to tell the difference is measurement, not intuition — which is the through-line connecting this section to the evaluation section later.

children.title: Retrieval and Knowledge
children.text:
The context window is finite and your knowledge is not. That single mismatch is the entire reason retrieval exists. A model's weights are frozen at a training cutoff and contain nothing about your documents, your tickets, or last week's policy change, and you cannot fit a corpus into a prompt. So you need a mechanism that, given a question, selects the small slice of your knowledge that bears on it and places that slice in the context.

There is a deeper justification than fitting, and it connects back to how the model fails. Answering from weights is a recall operation, which models do unreliably and hallucinate around. Answering from text present in the context is closer to a copying operation, which models do very well. Retrieval is therefore not merely a workaround for a size limit — it converts the model's weakest mode of operation into its strongest one, which is why it improves factual accuracy so dramatically.

The mechanism rests on embeddings: a learned map from text into a vector space where semantic similarity becomes geometric proximity. Once documents and queries live in the same space, finding relevant material becomes a nearest-neighbour search, which is a problem with well-understood, fast solutions. That is what a vector index provides.

The critical thing to hold onto is that retrieval is a separate system with its own failure modes, and most disappointing RAG deployments are failing at retrieval rather than at generation. If the right chunk was never fetched, no prompt engineering downstream can recover it — the model is simply answering a question whose evidence is absent. This section therefore treats retrieval as its own engineering problem: how text becomes vectors, how it is split, how search is performed, and how you measure whether the right material actually came back.

children.title: Embeddings and Vector Space
children.text:
An embedding model maps a piece of text to a fixed-length vector of numbers, typically a few hundred to a few thousand dimensions, with one property that makes the whole thing useful: texts with similar meaning land near each other. The mapping is learned, usually by training on pairs of related texts with an objective that pulls related pairs together and pushes unrelated ones apart.

This is what makes semantic search possible at all. Keyword search matches strings, so a query about cancelling a subscription misses a document titled ending your plan. In embedding space those two phrases sit close together because the training objective made them close, and the match is found through geometry rather than through shared characters.

Similarity is nearly always measured as cosine similarity — the angle between two vectors, ignoring their magnitude. The reason to prefer angle over distance is that magnitude in these spaces tends to correlate with incidental properties like text length and token frequency rather than with meaning, so normalising it away gives a cleaner signal. Most embedding models return already-normalised vectors, in which case cosine similarity and the dot product are the same computation.

Two constraints follow immediately and are non-negotiable in practice. Queries and documents must be embedded by the same model, since two models produce incompatible coordinate systems and comparing across them yields noise that looks like weak results. And changing your embedding model means re-embedding the entire corpus, because the old vectors are meaningless in the new space — a migration cost that scales with corpus size and should be weighed before you commit.
children.deep_text:
It is worth being clear about what the vector encodes, because over-trusting it is a common source of retrieval bugs. It encodes an aggregate impression of the passage, compressed to a fixed length regardless of input size. That compression is lossy in a specific and predictable way: distinctive but locally-scoped details — a version number, an account identifier, a single negation — contribute little to a vector dominated by the passage's overall topic. This is the mechanical reason dense retrieval underperforms on exact-match queries. Searching for error code E4021 may return many documents about errors and miss the one document that names that code, because the code is a small part of that document's overall meaning. It is not a tuning problem; it is what averaging into a fixed-length vector does, and it is why hybrid search exists.

Negation is the sharpest illustration. The vector for a passage that says the feature is available and one that says the feature is not available are close, because they share nearly all their semantic content and differ by one token whose contribution is diluted. Semantic similarity is not logical equivalence, and any application where the polarity of a statement matters — compliance, medical guidance, policy lookup — cannot rely on embedding similarity alone to distinguish them.

Model choice comes down to four axes and one hidden trap. The axes are quality on retrieval benchmarks, dimensionality, cost, and maximum input length. Higher dimensionality generally captures more nuance and costs more in storage and search time; some modern models support truncating dimensions with graceful quality degradation, which is a genuinely useful tuning knob. Maximum input length interacts directly with chunking: an embedding model that accepts 512 tokens silently truncates anything longer, so a 2000-token chunk is embedded from its first quarter and the rest is invisible to search. That silent truncation is the hidden trap, and it produces a baffling symptom where content that is definitely in the corpus is never retrieved.

Domain mismatch deserves attention because it explains disappointing results on specialised corpora. General-purpose embedding models are trained mostly on web text, where the fine distinctions of a legal, clinical, or internal-engineering vocabulary are not well represented. Two terms of art that a specialist knows are opposites can be near-identical to a general model. The remedies, in ascending order of effort, are domain-specific embedding models where they exist, hybrid search to let lexical matching carry the specialised vocabulary, and fine-tuning an embedding model on your own query-document pairs, which is achievable with a few thousand examples and often produces the largest single improvement available on a specialised corpus.

Two operational practices are worth adopting from the start. First, store the embedding model identifier and version alongside every vector, so that a mixed-model index is detectable rather than mysterious — this failure produces subtly degraded results with no error, and without the metadata it is close to undiagnosable. Second, plan for re-embedding as a routine operation with a dual-write or shadow-index path, not as an emergency migration. Embedding models improve, and a corpus you cannot re-embed without downtime is a corpus frozen on whichever model you happened to pick first.

interview.question: Why does semantic search often fail on exact identifiers like error codes or SKUs?
interview.answer: Because embedding compresses a whole passage into a fixed-length vector dominated by its overall topic, so a rare token contributes little to the result. A document containing error code E4021 is, in vector space, mostly a document about errors, so a query for that exact code retrieves topical neighbours instead. The standard fix is hybrid search: run lexical retrieval such as BM25 alongside the dense search and fuse the rankings, since exact-term matching is precisely what sparse retrieval is good at.

interview.question: What happens if you embed documents with one model and queries with another?
interview.answer: The vectors live in unrelated coordinate systems, so similarity scores are effectively noise. The dangerous part is that nothing errors — you get plausible-looking scores and rankings that are meaningless, which surfaces as generally poor answers rather than as a bug. Storing the embedding model identifier with every vector makes this detectable, and it is worth doing from day one because the alternative is an extremely difficult diagnosis.

interview.question: Why might embedding similarity fail to distinguish 'the feature is supported' from 'the feature is not supported'?
interview.answer: Because the two passages share almost all their semantic content and differ by a single token whose contribution is diluted by the averaging into a fixed-length vector. Embedding similarity approximates topical relatedness, not logical equivalence. In any domain where polarity is load-bearing — policy, compliance, clinical guidance — retrieval must be supplemented by lexical signals, by chunking that keeps the qualifying clause with its subject, or by a verification step after generation.

children.title: Chunking Strategies
children.text:
Documents have to be split before they can be embedded, and the split determines what retrieval can possibly return. This is the most consequential decision in a RAG pipeline and it is routinely made by accepting a library default, which is roughly like choosing a database index at random.

The tension is structural rather than a matter of tuning. A chunk plays two roles at once. As the unit of retrieval it wants to be small and focused, because a small chunk is about one thing and its embedding is a sharp representation of that thing. As the unit of context it wants to be large, because the model needs enough surrounding material to interpret what it was given. Optimising for one degrades the other, and there is no size that is best for both.

Small chunks retrieve precisely and then hand the model orphaned fragments — a sentence saying it must be enabled in the console, with no indication of what it refers to. Large chunks carry their context but blur their embeddings, since a passage covering four topics has a vector that is near none of them, and they waste tokens by attaching a lot of irrelevant text to every hit.

The decisive insight is that document structure usually resolves the tension better than any character count. Splitting on semantic boundaries — sections, headings, function definitions, list items — produces chunks that are internally coherent because the author already grouped related material. Fixed-size splitting ignores that structure and cuts through the middle of arguments, tables, and code blocks. And the two roles can be decoupled entirely by embedding a small unit for search while returning a larger surrounding unit for context, which is the technique that dissolves the trade-off rather than compromising on it.
children.deep_text:
Work through what fixed-size character splitting does to a real document and the problem becomes concrete. Take a technical manual chunked at a thousand characters. One chunk ends mid-sentence in the middle of a procedure. The next begins with the second half of that sentence and continues into an unrelated section. A table is cut across three chunks, so no chunk contains both the column headers and the row a user asks about, and the retrieved row is a set of unlabelled numbers. A code example is severed from the explanation of what it does. None of this errors, and all of it degrades answers in ways that look like the model being unhelpful.

Overlap is the usual first mitigation: let consecutive chunks share a hundred or two hundred characters so a boundary-straddling fact appears whole in at least one of them. It works, and it costs storage and introduces near-duplicate results that consume slots in your top-k with the same information. It is a patch on fixed-size splitting rather than a solution, and it becomes unnecessary once splitting follows structure.

Structure-aware splitting is the better default and is usually straightforward. Markdown and HTML have headings; code has functions, classes, and modules; PDFs of any quality have sections; transcripts have speaker turns and timestamps. Split at those boundaries and each chunk is a unit the author intended to be coherent. Then apply a size cap with a fallback split for the occasional oversized section, rather than making size the primary criterion. The additional move that costs almost nothing and pays consistently is to prepend the ancestry of each chunk — document title, chapter, section heading — to its text before embedding.
