A chunk that begins Billing / Refunds / Eligibility embeds far more distinctively than the same paragraph alone, and the improvement in retrieval is often larger than any change of embedding model.

The techniques that genuinely decouple the two roles are worth knowing by name because they solve the underlying tension rather than trading against it. Small-to-big retrieval embeds a small precise unit, typically a sentence or a paragraph, but returns the parent section when that unit is retrieved, so search is sharp and context is complete. The hypothetical-question technique embeds generated questions that a chunk answers, which closes the gap between the interrogative form of queries and the declarative form of documents — a real mismatch, since a user asks how do I rotate credentials while the document says credential rotation is performed via the console. Contextual retrieval prepends a short model-generated description of how each chunk relates to its document before embedding, which is more expensive at index time and measurably effective.

Chunk size interacts with everything downstream, which is why it should be evaluated rather than argued about. It sets how many chunks fit in your context budget at a given top-k, so halving chunk size lets you retrieve twice as many for the same tokens. It interacts with the embedding model's maximum input length, beyond which content is silently truncated and effectively unsearchable. It interacts with reranking, since rerankers score a query against a passage and perform better on focused passages than sprawling ones. The only defensible way to choose is empirically: build a small set of real questions with known correct source passages, then measure retrieval recall across several chunking configurations. That experiment takes an afternoon and is more valuable than weeks of prompt adjustment downstream, because no prompt can compensate for a chunk that was never a coherent unit in the first place.

interview.question: Why is there no single best chunk size?
interview.answer: Because a chunk serves two roles with opposing requirements. As the unit of retrieval it should be small and topically focused so its embedding is a sharp representation; as the unit of context it should be large enough that the model can interpret it. Any single size compromises one or the other. The techniques that actually resolve this decouple the roles — embed a small unit for search and return its larger parent for context — rather than searching for a compromise value.

interview.question: How would you evaluate a chunking change?
interview.answer: With a labelled retrieval set, independent of the generation step. Collect real questions and mark which source passages contain the answers, then measure recall at k and mean reciprocal rank across chunking configurations. Judging by reading a handful of final answers conflates retrieval quality with generation quality and gives no signal about which stage changed. Retrieval is a component and deserves component-level metrics.

interview.question: What is the cheapest high-impact improvement to a naive chunking pipeline?
interview.answer: Prepending structural context — document title and heading path — to each chunk before embedding. It is a few lines of code, it costs almost no tokens, and it substantially sharpens the vector by disambiguating a paragraph that would otherwise be generic. A paragraph about eligibility is nearly meaningless in isolation; the same paragraph tagged Billing / Refunds / Eligibility is distinctive, and retrieval improves accordingly. Structure-aware splitting instead of fixed-character splitting is the natural next step.

children.title: Hybrid Search and Reranking
children.text:
Once vectors exist they have to be searched, and at any real corpus size exact nearest-neighbour search is too slow — comparing a query against every vector is linear in corpus size. Vector indexes use approximate nearest neighbour algorithms, most commonly HNSW, which builds a navigable graph and searches it greedily, trading a small and tunable amount of recall for orders-of-magnitude speed.

More important than the index is the recognition that dense retrieval alone has a systematic blind spot. Because embeddings encode aggregate meaning, they are weak exactly where a query hinges on a rare, exact token: a product code, an error identifier, a person's surname, an API method name. Sparse retrieval — BM25 and its relatives, which score on term overlap weighted by term rarity — is strong precisely there and weak on paraphrase, which is where dense retrieval is strong.

The two are complementary rather than competing, and hybrid search runs both and fuses the rankings, typically with reciprocal rank fusion, which combines by rank position and so avoids the problem that cosine scores and BM25 scores are not on comparable scales. Hybrid is the sensible default for most production systems, not an optimisation to add later.

Reranking then adds a second stage with a different cost profile. First-stage retrieval must be fast because it scores the whole corpus, so it compares independently-computed vectors. A cross-encoder reranker instead reads the query and a candidate passage together and scores their relevance directly, which is far more accurate and far too slow to run over a corpus — but entirely practical over the fifty candidates the first stage returned. Retrieve broadly and cheaply, then rerank narrowly and precisely, is the standard high-performing architecture.
children.deep_text:
Understanding why a cross-encoder beats an embedding comparison clarifies the whole two-stage design. Embedding retrieval is a bi-encoder: query and document are encoded separately, without ever seeing each other, and compared by geometry. That independence is exactly what makes it scalable, since document vectors are computed once at index time and reused for every query forever. A cross-encoder concatenates query and passage into one input and runs a full attention pass over both together, so every query token can attend to every passage token and the model can judge whether this specific passage answers this specific question. That interaction is why it is more accurate, and the requirement to run a forward pass per query-document pair is why it cannot scale past a candidate list. The architecture is forced by the cost structure, not chosen by preference.

Metadata filtering is the operationally critical feature that gets underweighted in discussions of retrieval quality. Most real queries are implicitly scoped — this user's documents, this workspace, this product version, documents not yet archived — and enforcing that scope is both a correctness and a security requirement. The subtlety is where the filter is applied. Pre-filtering restricts the candidate set before the vector search, which is correct but can degrade the ANN index's performance badly when the filter is highly selective, because the graph's connectivity assumes the full node set. Post-filtering searches first and then discards non-matching results, which is fast but can return far fewer than k results, or none, when the filter is selective. Serious vector databases implement filtered search that pushes the predicate into the graph traversal. If you are enforcing tenant isolation, verify how your engine does this, because a post-filter that returns zero results for a small tenant is a functional bug and a pre-filter implemented naively is a performance cliff.

HNSW's parameters deserve to be understood rather than defaulted, since they are the actual latency-recall dial. Construction parameters control graph connectivity and build-time search breadth, trading index build time and memory for better recall. The query-time breadth parameter directly trades latency for recall and can be tuned per query, which is often the right move: use a low value for a latency-sensitive autocomplete path and a high value for a thorough research query against the same index. Because these are approximate methods, measuring recall against exact search on a sample is a worthwhile one-off exercise — a common surprise is that a default configuration is losing ten or fifteen percent of true nearest neighbours, which manifests downstream as the answer is sometimes missing for no apparent reason.

Query transformation is the underused lever on the input side. Users write short, ambiguous, context-dependent queries, especially in a conversation where the third message is just what about refunds. Rewriting the query with the conversation context before embedding it resolves that reference and typically produces a large improvement for the cost of one small model call. Related techniques include generating multiple query variants and merging results, which improves recall on ambiguous questions, and HyDE, which generates a hypothetical answer and embeds that instead of the question — exploiting the fact that a hypothetical answer sits closer in vector space to real answers than a question does.

Finally, be deliberate about how many chunks you keep. More retrieved context is not monotonically better: beyond a point you are adding marginally relevant material that dilutes attention, pushes the truly relevant chunk toward the middle of the context where it is least attended, and costs tokens on every request. This is where reranking pays twice — it lets you retrieve a wide candidate set for recall and then pass only the few genuinely best chunks for precision, so the final context is both more likely to contain the answer and less cluttered around it. Choosing that final k by measurement rather than by intuition is one of the more reliable improvements available.

interview.question: Why combine BM25 with vector search instead of picking the better one?
interview.answer: Because their failure modes are complementary. Dense retrieval handles paraphrase and synonymy but dilutes rare exact tokens into an aggregate vector, so it misses identifiers, codes, and proper nouns. BM25 matches exact terms weighted by rarity, which is exactly that case, but fails when the query and document share meaning without sharing words. Fusing the two rankings — usually by reciprocal rank fusion, since raw scores are on incomparable scales — recovers both strengths, which is why hybrid is a sensible default rather than an optimisation.

interview.question: Why can a reranker not simply replace first-stage retrieval?
interview.answer: Because it requires a forward pass for every query-document pair. A cross-encoder reads query and passage jointly, which is what makes it accurate, but it means scoring a million-document corpus would need a million forward passes per query. The bi-encoder first stage is cheap because document vectors are precomputed once and reused. The two-stage design is forced by that cost asymmetry: retrieve broadly with the cheap method, then rerank a small candidate list with the expensive one.

interview.question: A multi-tenant RAG system occasionally returns nothing for smaller tenants. What do you suspect?
interview.answer: Post-filtering. The vector search runs over the whole index, returns its top k, and the tenant filter is applied afterwards — so for a tenant holding a small fraction of the corpus, few or none of the global top k belong to them. The fix is filtered search that pushes the tenant predicate into the index traversal, or pre-filtering with an index that supports it efficiently. This is also a security-relevant path, so the filter must be enforced in the engine rather than trusted to the application layer.

children.title: Measuring Retrieval Quality
children.text:
RAG systems fail at retrieval far more often than at generation, and teams routinely misdiagnose this because they only ever look at the final answer. A bad answer produced from the wrong documents looks exactly like a bad answer produced from the right ones. Without separating the stages you end up rewriting prompts to fix a problem that lives in the index.

The fix is to measure retrieval as its own component against its own labelled set. Collect real questions, identify which passages actually contain the answers, and then measure whether retrieval returned them. Recall at k asks whether the correct passage appeared in the top k at all, which is the ceiling on everything downstream — if it was not retrieved, no amount of generation quality can recover it. Precision and mean reciprocal rank tell you how much irrelevant material came with it and how highly the right one ranked.

That decomposition turns a vague complaint into a decision. If recall at ten is ninety percent but the right chunk usually ranks eighth, you have a ranking problem and a reranker is the answer. If recall at ten is fifty percent, ranking is irrelevant — your chunking, your embedding model, or your query handling is losing the material entirely, and reranking a candidate list that lacks the answer cannot help.

The complementary generation-side metrics are groundedness and answer relevance: whether every claim in the answer is supported by the retrieved passages, and whether the answer addresses the question. Together with retrieval recall these three localise almost any failure. Low recall is a retrieval bug; high recall with low groundedness means the model is ignoring good context or padding from weights; high groundedness with low relevance means you retrieved and faithfully summarised the wrong thing.
children.deep_text:
The practical obstacle is always the labelled set, and the standard objection — we do not have one and cannot afford to build one — is worth confronting because it is usually wrong about the cost. A useful evaluation set is not thousands of examples. Fifty to a hundred real questions with their correct source passages identified is enough to detect meaningful regressions and to compare configurations, and it can be assembled in a day or two by pulling genuine questions from support tickets, search logs, or user sessions. The critical property is that questions come from real usage rather than from an engineer's imagination, because engineers write well-formed questions about material they know exists, and users write terse, ambiguous, misspelled questions about material that may not exist at all.

Synthetic generation offers a fast bootstrap with an important caveat. Take each chunk, ask a model to generate questions it answers, and you have query-passage pairs immediately, at scale, for very little effort. The caveat is that these questions are generated from the chunk and therefore tend to reuse its vocabulary, which makes retrieval look easier than it is — you have built a test set biased toward lexical overlap. It is a legitimate starting point and a floor rather than a measurement, and it should be replaced or supplemented with real queries as they accumulate.

Groundedness measurement is where LLM-as-judge earns its place, since checking whether each claim in an answer is supported by the provided passages is a task models do reasonably well when framed carefully. The framing that works is decompositional: split the answer into atomic claims, then for each claim ask a judge, given only the retrieved passages, whether it is supported, contradicted, or unaddressed. Asking for a single holistic groundedness score produces a number that drifts and correlates poorly with human judgement; asking for per-claim verdicts produces something you can inspect, and it points at the specific unsupported sentence rather than at the answer as a whole. Requiring citations at generation time makes this cheaper still, because verification becomes a check that cited spans exist and support the claim.

A failure mode this measurement catches and nothing else does is the unanswerable question. When the corpus does not contain an answer, retrieval still returns its top k — the nearest neighbours of the query, however far away — and a model handed plausible-looking but irrelevant context will frequently synthesise an answer from it. Every evaluation set should therefore include questions with no answer in the corpus, where the correct behaviour is an explicit refusal. Systems that are never tested on these almost always fail them, because nothing in the design distinguishes weak retrieval from good retrieval; the similarity score is relative, not absolute. An absolute relevance threshold below which you decline to answer is the standard control, and it can only be calibrated with exactly this kind of labelled negative set.

Finally, instrument production rather than relying only on offline sets. Log the query, the retrieved chunk identifiers with their scores, and the final answer, for every request. That log makes it possible to answer why did it say that for any individual complaint by inspecting what was actually retrieved, and in aggregate it reveals patterns that offline evaluation misses — queries with uniformly low top scores, indicating a gap in the corpus; chunks that are retrieved constantly across unrelated queries, which usually means a chunk of boilerplate whose embedding sits near the centre of the space and should be removed; and query clusters where users repeatedly rephrase, which is a reliable signal of retrieval failure without any labelling at all.

interview.question: How do you tell whether a RAG failure is in retrieval or generation?
interview.answer: Measure them separately. Check recall at k against a labelled set: did the passage containing the answer appear in what was retrieved? If not, it is a retrieval failure and no prompt change can fix it. If it did appear and the answer is still wrong, measure groundedness — whether each claim is supported by the retrieved passages — to determine whether the model ignored good context or drifted into recalling from weights. Looking only at final answers cannot distinguish these two cases.

interview.question: Your corpus does not contain the answer to a question. What does the system do, and what should it do?
interview.answer: By default it retrieves the nearest neighbours anyway — similarity is relative, so something always comes back — and the model synthesises an answer from irrelevant but plausible context. It should recognise insufficiency and decline. That requires an absolute relevance threshold below which you do not answer, plus an explicit instruction and schema path for refusal. Calibrating the threshold requires an evaluation set that deliberately includes unanswerable questions, which most teams never build, which is why most systems fail this case.

interview.question: You have no labelled evaluation data. How do you start?
interview.answer: Pull fifty to a hundred real questions from support tickets, search logs, or session transcripts and mark which passages answer them — that is a day or two of work and enough to detect regressions and compare configurations. Synthetic questions generated from chunks are a faster bootstrap but are biased toward the chunk's own vocabulary, so they overstate retrieval quality and should be treated as a floor. In parallel, start logging queries, retrieved chunk ids, and scores in production, since that log becomes the source of both real evaluation questions and aggregate failure signals.

children.deep_text:
The structure of this section follows the pipeline, and the pipeline is worth naming explicitly because failures are localised to stages. Documents are chunked, chunks are embedded, embeddings are indexed. At query time the query is embedded, the index returns candidates, candidates may be reranked, and the survivors are assembled into the context. Six stages, each of which can independently ruin the result, and a system that reports only end-to-end answer quality tells you nothing about which one is broken.

The first unit covers embeddings themselves: what the vector actually represents, why cosine similarity is the standard measure, what similarity does and does not capture, and the practical constraints — model choice, dimensionality, the absolute requirement that queries and documents be embedded by the same model, and the migration cost of changing that model later.

The second covers chunking, which is the least glamorous and most consequential decision in the whole pipeline. A chunk is simultaneously the unit of retrieval and the unit of context, and those two roles want different sizes. Chunk too small and you retrieve precisely but hand the model fragments without the surrounding context needed to interpret them; chunk too large and every retrieval drags in mostly-irrelevant text that dilutes attention and costs tokens.

The third covers search itself: approximate nearest neighbour indexes and why exact search does not scale, the complementary strengths of dense and sparse retrieval, hybrid fusion, metadata filtering, and reranking as a second-stage precision pass. The recurring theme is that pure semantic search has a specific blind spot around exact identifiers and rare terms, which is exactly where users often need it most.

The fourth covers evaluation of retrieval as a component, separate from the answer. This is the unit that changes how teams work, because it converts a vague complaint that the assistant is not very good into a precise measurement of whether the correct document was in the top five, which is answerable and fixable.

Read this section knowing that it is context engineering with a query-time selection step bolted on. Everything from the previous section still applies to what you do with the retrieved material once you have it.

children.title: Agents and Tool Use
children.text:
Everything up to this point produces text. An agent is what you get when that text is allowed to cause effects — when the model's output is parsed, matched against a set of declared functions, executed, and the result fed back so the model can decide what to do next. The model itself never executes anything; it emits a structured request, and your code decides whether to honour it.

That framing matters because it locates the entire trust boundary. The model is a planner that proposes; your runtime is the executor that disposes. Every safety property an agent has comes from constraints in the executor, never from instructions in the prompt, because the prompt is advisory and the executor is the thing that actually holds the credentials.

Three problems arrive the moment you close that loop, and none of them exist in single-turn generation. The loop has no inherent termination condition, so it can cycle indefinitely, retrying a failing call or oscillating between two states. Errors compound multiplicatively: a chain of ten steps each ninety-five percent reliable succeeds end to end only about sixty percent of the time, so per-step accuracy that sounds excellent produces a system that usually fails. And the cost of a mistake is no longer a bad paragraph — it is a sent email, a deleted row, a charged card.

So agent engineering is mostly the discipline of constraint. Bound the iterations, bound the blast radius of each tool, make failures observable rather than silent, and prefer the least agentic architecture that solves the problem. A fixed pipeline you can reason about beats a free-running loop that occasionally does something brilliant and occasionally does something expensive.

children.title: Tool Calling Mechanics
children.text:
A tool definition is three things: a name, a natural-language description, and a JSON schema for the arguments. You send these with the request; the model may reply with a structured call naming a tool and supplying arguments that conform to the schema. Constrained decoding usually guarantees the arguments are schema-valid, which is a real guarantee and a narrow one — valid does not mean correct or sensible.

The consequence engineers underestimate is that tool descriptions are prompt engineering, not documentation. The description is the model's entire basis for deciding when the tool applies. A description reading searches the database gives it nothing to discriminate on, and the model will call it for questions it cannot answer and skip it for questions it can. A description stating when to use it, when not to, and what it returns turns tool selection from guesswork into something close to deterministic.

Schema design does the same work for arguments. Enums beat free-text strings because they make an invalid value unrepresentable rather than merely discouraged. Required fields force the model to obtain information rather than inventing a plausible default. Descriptions on individual parameters resolve ambiguities — a date field annotated with its expected format and timezone gets the right value; the same field bare gets whatever the model guesses.

The other structural lever is the size of the toolset. Selection accuracy degrades as the number of tools grows and as their boundaries blur, because the model is discriminating among descriptions. Ten well-separated tools work well; fifty overlapping ones produce confident wrong choices. Merging near-duplicates, or retrieving a relevant subset of tools per request, restores accuracy more reliably than any amount of prompt exhortation.
children.deep_text:
The most useful mental correction here is that a tool call is a request, not an action. The model emits an intention; nothing has happened yet. Your executor sits between the intention and the effect, and that gap is where every control lives — authorisation, validation, rate limiting, confirmation, audit logging. Systems that get compromised are almost always systems that collapsed this gap, wiring model output directly into execution because the loop was simpler to write that way. Keeping the gap explicit costs a few lines and is the difference between a bug and an incident.

Argument validation must therefore be real validation, not schema conformance. The schema guarantees the shape; it says nothing about whether the values are permissible. A schema-valid call can specify a user id belonging to someone else, an amount larger than any legitimate transaction, a file path outside the allowed directory, or a query that would return the entire table. The executor must check each of those against the actual authorisation context of the request — which is to say, against the identity of the human on whose behalf the agent is acting, not against anything the model said. If the model can name a resource, your executor must independently confirm that this session is entitled to it.

Tool results are context, which has two practical consequences. First, results consume tokens and accumulate across iterations, so a tool that returns an entire API payload can exhaust the context in a handful of calls; return the fields that matter, paginated, with a summary rather than a dump. Second, results are how the model learns what happened, so error results need to be informative and actionable. A result reading Error: 400 tells the model nothing and it will typically retry the identical call. A result reading the start_date parameter must be ISO 8601, for example 2024-03-01; you supplied March 1st lets it self-correct on the next iteration, which converts a hard failure into a recoverable one. Well-written error strings are among the highest-leverage things in an agent codebase and they are almost never treated that way.

Parallel tool calling is worth designing for explicitly. Modern models can emit several independent calls in a single turn, and executing them concurrently collapses what would be several sequential round trips into one. The gain is large — each round trip includes a full model call — but it requires your executor to handle a list of calls rather than one, and it requires the tools to be genuinely independent. Where a call depends on a previous result the model must sequence it, and tool descriptions that state such dependencies help it do so correctly.

Finally, a design instinct worth carrying: prefer coarse tools that accomplish a meaningful unit of work over fine-grained tools that mirror your internal API surface. Exposing eight primitives that must be composed in exact order asks the model to reconstruct a procedure you already know, and each composition step is another opportunity for the multiplicative reliability problem to bite. One tool named schedule_meeting that internally checks availability, resolves attendees, and creates the event is far more reliable than three tools the model must chain — because you wrote the chaining logic in code where it is deterministic, tested, and free.

interview.question: The model keeps choosing the wrong tool. Where do you look first?
interview.answer: At the tool descriptions and the size of the toolset, before touching the system prompt. Descriptions are the model's only basis for discrimination, so overlapping or vague ones make the decision ambiguous by construction. I would rewrite each to state when to use it, when not to, and what it returns, then look for near-duplicate tools to merge. If there are dozens, I would retrieve a relevant subset per request instead of sending all of them, since selection accuracy degrades with count.

interview.question: Constrained decoding guarantees schema-valid arguments. What does that not guarantee?
interview.answer: That the values are correct or permitted. Shape validity says nothing about semantics or authorisation: a schema-valid call can reference another tenant's record, specify an out-of-range amount, or point at a path outside the allowed root. The executor has to validate values against the actual authorisation context of the human the agent is acting for, independently of anything the model produced. The model proposes; only the executor holds credentials.

interview.question: Why does error message wording matter more in an agent than in a normal API?
interview.answer: Because the error is fed back into the context and becomes the model's sole information about what went wrong. A bare status code gives it nothing to act on, so it typically retries the same call and burns iterations. An error that names the offending parameter, the expected format, and an example lets the model self-correct on the next turn, converting a terminal failure into a recovered one. Error strings in an agent are prompt surface, and it is worth writing them as such.

children.title: The Agent Loop
children.text:
The loop is simple to write and easy to get wrong: call the model, and if it returned a tool call, execute it, append the result, and call again; otherwise return the text. What that omits is every termination condition, and a loop without them is a program that can run until your budget is gone.

Non-termination is not exotic. A model that receives an unhelpful error retries the identical call. Two tools whose results contradict each other produce oscillation. A task that is genuinely impossible with the available tools yields indefinite attempts, because nothing in the loop tells the model to give up. Each of these is a normal Tuesday, not an edge case, and each is prevented by a hard iteration cap enforced in your code rather than requested in the prompt.

Budgets should be plural, because iterations are a weak proxy for the thing you actually care about. Cap iterations, cap wall-clock time, cap total tokens, cap spend, and cap invocations of individually expensive or dangerous tools. Any single limit leaves an obvious hole: ten iterations is cheap with small tool results and ruinous with large ones.

The other half is what happens at the boundary. Hitting a limit is a state your system must handle deliberately, not an exception to swallow — return the partial work, say plainly that the task was not completed, and preserve enough state that a human or a retry can resume. An agent that silently returns its last partial thought as if it were a finished answer is worse than one that fails loudly, because the failure becomes invisible to everyone downstream.
children.deep_text:
Context growth is the loop's quiet structural problem. Every iteration appends the model's message and the tool result, and the entire history is re-sent on every call. That makes cost grow quadratically in the number of steps: step one sends a small context, step twenty sends everything that came before. A long-running agent can spend most of its money re-reading its own transcript. Three mitigations are standard, and they compose. Truncate or summarise old tool results, since the raw payload from step three is rarely needed at step eighteen while its conclusion may be. Externalise state — have the agent write findings to a scratchpad or file it can re-read on demand, rather than carrying everything in context. And structure prefixes so prompt caching applies, since a stable system prompt and tool definitions at the front of every request are exactly the cacheable case.

Failure taxonomy should drive handling rather than a blanket retry. A transient infrastructure error is the executor's problem and should be retried with backoff without ever entering the context, since the model has nothing useful to contribute. A malformed-argument error is the model's problem and should go back to it with a message specific enough to correct. A permission error is neither and is usually terminal — retrying will not grant access, and the correct behaviour is to stop and report what was denied. Collapsing these into one path produces the common pathology where an agent spends its entire iteration budget retrying an operation it was never authorised to perform.

Observability is not optional here, because an agent failure is a trajectory rather than a stack trace. When someone reports that it did the wrong thing, the only way to answer why is to replay the sequence of model outputs, tool calls, arguments, and results. That means structured tracing of every step with timing and token counts, spans linked into a single trace per request, and enough retention to investigate a complaint from last week. Teams that add this after their first production incident always say they should have had it from the start; the cost is a day and the alternative is debugging by guesswork.

Human-in-the-loop belongs in the design from the beginning rather than being retrofitted after something goes wrong. The natural boundary is reversibility: reads and idempotent operations proceed automatically, while anything that sends, charges, deletes, or publishes pauses for confirmation. Implementing this well means the loop must be suspendable — able to serialise its state, wait an arbitrary time for an out-of-band approval, and resume — which is a meaningfully different architecture from a synchronous while loop and is very awkward to add later. Deciding early whether you need it is one of the higher-leverage architectural calls in the whole section.

A subtler failure worth naming is the confidently wrong completion. The loop terminates normally, the model produces a fluent final answer, and the answer is based on a tool call that returned nothing or errored in a way the model glossed over. Nothing in the loop distinguishes this from success. The defences are a verification step that checks the final answer against the actual tool results, and instrumentation that flags trajectories where a tool returned an error or an empty result but the final answer asserted a conclusion anyway. That pattern is common, it is invisible to end-to-end success metrics, and it is exactly what erodes user trust.

interview.question: Why do agent loops need multiple budgets rather than just a maximum iteration count?
interview.answer: Because iterations are a poor proxy for cost. Ten iterations with small tool results is trivial; ten with large payloads can consume an enormous number of tokens, since the whole history is re-sent every turn. Wall-clock time matters independently for user-facing latency, and specific dangerous or expensive tools deserve their own caps. Any single limit leaves a hole that some real trajectory will find, so iterations, time, tokens, spend, and per-tool counts should all be bounded.

interview.question: Why does agent cost grow faster than linearly with the number of steps?
interview.answer: Because the model is stateless, so every call re-sends the entire accumulated conversation including all prior tool results. Step n pays for everything from steps one through n minus one, making total input tokens roughly quadratic in step count. Mitigations are summarising or truncating stale tool results, externalising state to a scratchpad the agent reads on demand, and arranging a stable prefix so prompt caching covers the system prompt and tool definitions.

interview.question: An agent finishes normally but its answer is wrong, and the trace shows a tool returned an error mid-run. How do you catch this class of failure?
interview.answer: Not with end-to-end success metrics, which record it as a success. You need a check that reconciles the final answer against the actual tool results, plus instrumentation that flags any trajectory where a tool errored or returned empty yet the final answer still asserted a conclusion. That pattern is a reliable signal of a confidently-wrong completion, and it is invisible unless you look for it specifically.

children.title: Agent Architecture Patterns
children.text:
Autonomy is a dial, and turning it up costs predictability. At the low end is a fixed chain: you wrote the sequence and the model fills in the steps. It is testable, its latency and cost are bounded, and it handles exactly the cases you anticipated. At the high end is an open loop with broad tool access, which handles cases you never enumerated and gives up your ability to say what it will do or what it will cost.

The decision rule that holds up is to use the least autonomy that solves the problem, because every increment buys flexibility with reliability. If a task always follows the same three steps, encode those three steps — asking a model to rediscover them on every request adds cost, latency, and several independent chances to go wrong, in exchange for nothing.

Between the extremes are the patterns worth knowing. Routing classifies the request and dispatches to a specialised handler, which keeps each handler's prompt and toolset small and sharp. Sequential chaining decomposes a task into stages where each stage's output is validated before the next begins, so errors are caught at the boundary instead of propagating. Evaluator-optimiser loops generate, critique, and revise, which works well where quality is judgeable and a first draft is rarely the best one.

Multi-agent architectures — a coordinator delegating to specialists — are genuinely useful when subtasks are independent and can run in parallel, or when their contexts would otherwise collide. They are frequently adopted for the wrong reason, because the org chart metaphor is appealing, and they add real cost: every delegation is a serialisation of context through natural language, which is lossy, slow, and expensive. A single well-prompted agent with the right tools beats a committee of specialists more often than the diagrams suggest.
children.deep_text:
The strongest argument for constraining autonomy is that it makes evaluation possible. A fixed chain has defined stages, so you can build a test set for each stage and know precisely where a regression came from. An open loop produces a different trajectory every run, so the only measurable thing is end-to-end outcome, and when that degrades you have no localisation. This is why teams that begin with an autonomous agent so often end up decomposing it — not because the agent could not do the task, but because they could not tell whether a change made it better, and without that they cannot safely change anything.

Where multi-agent genuinely pays is worth being specific about, because the pattern is neither useless nor a default. It pays when subtasks are truly independent and parallelisable — researching five companies concurrently is five times faster and the results do not interfere. It pays when contexts would otherwise contaminate each other, since an agent reasoning about one codebase area is cleaner without another area's details in its window. It pays when a subtask needs a genuinely different configuration: a different model, a different tool set, a different privilege level. That last one is an underrated security pattern — a narrow subagent that can read untrusted web content but holds no credentials, reporting back to a coordinator that holds them, is a real boundary rather than a rhetorical one.

Where it does not pay is when the subtasks are sequential and interdependent, which is most of the time. In that case delegation adds a full serialisation and deserialisation of state through natural language at every hop, and information is lost at each one. A specialist that returns a summary has discarded the details the coordinator might have needed, and the coordinator cannot know what was discarded. The rule of thumb that survives contact with production is that a shared context beats a delegated one whenever the work is genuinely coupled.

Reflection deserves a caveat that is often omitted. Asking a model to critique and revise its own output improves quality on tasks with judgeable criteria — code that must compile, text that must satisfy an explicit rubric — and is close to useless where the model's critique is drawn from the same distribution as its generation. If it could not tell the fact was wrong when writing it, asking it to check will not usually reveal that either. Reflection is most valuable when the critique step has access to something the generation step lacked: test results, a linter, retrieved evidence, or a rubric it did not see. Without new information, self-critique mostly adds latency and cost while producing longer, more hedged output.

The pattern that most reliably improves real agent systems is the least architectural: give the agent fewer, better tools and a clearer objective. The majority of production agent failures trace to ambiguous task definition, overlapping tool descriptions, or missing information in the context, not to insufficient architectural sophistication. Before adding a planner, a critic, and three specialists, it is nearly always worth checking whether one agent with four well-described tools and an unambiguous objective does the job — because it usually does, and it is dramatically easier to evaluate, debug, and afford.

interview.question: When is a multi-agent architecture actually the right choice?
interview.answer: When subtasks are genuinely independent and benefit from parallelism, when separate contexts prevent contamination, or when a subtask needs a different model, toolset, or privilege level. That last case is a real security pattern — an unprivileged subagent handles untrusted content while the coordinator holds the credentials. When subtasks are sequential and interdependent, delegation just serialises state through natural language at every hop and loses information, and a single agent with a shared context does better.

interview.question: Why does more autonomy make a system harder to improve, not just harder to predict?
interview.answer: Because it destroys localisation. A fixed chain has stages you can test individually, so a regression points at a stage. An open loop takes a different trajectory each run, leaving only end-to-end outcome as a signal, so when quality drops you cannot tell which change caused it. Teams often decompose autonomous agents not because the agent failed the task but because they could not measure it, and without measurement they could not safely change anything.

interview.question: When does asking a model to critique its own output help, and when is it theatre?
interview.answer: It helps when the critique step has information the generation step lacked — test results, compiler output, a linter, retrieved evidence, an explicit rubric it had not seen. It is theatre when the critique draws on the same knowledge as the generation, because a factual error the model did not notice while writing is unlikely to be caught by asking the same model to look again. In that case reflection adds latency and cost and tends to produce longer, more hedged output rather than more correct output.

children.title: Agent Security and Blast Radius
children.text:
Combine three ingredients and you have a security problem rather than a feature: a model that follows instructions in its context, a context assembled partly from untrusted sources, and tools that act on the world with real credentials. Prompt injection is not a bug in a particular model — it is what follows from a component that cannot distinguish instructions it was given from instructions it merely read.

The mechanism is worth stating plainly. The model sees one flat sequence of tokens. Your system prompt, the user's question, a retrieved document, and a web page fetched mid-task all arrive as text, and nothing marks which of them carries authority. A web page containing a line that instructs the reader to email the conversation history to an address is, from the model's position, indistinguishable in kind from your own instructions. Delimiters and warnings raise the difficulty; they do not change the underlying situation.

Because the boundary cannot be enforced inside the model, it has to be enforced outside it. The controls that work are ordinary security engineering. The agent runs with the permissions of the human it acts for, never with an ambient service account. Tools are scoped to the minimum that the task requires. Irreversible actions require confirmation from the human rather than from the model. Outbound destinations are allowlisted, since exfiltration needs a channel and removing the channel removes the risk.

The useful mental exercise is to assume injection succeeds and ask what it gets. If a hostile instruction inside a retrieved document could cause an email to be sent, a record to be deleted, or data to leave the system, the design is unsafe regardless of how carefully the prompt is worded. If the worst outcome is a wrong answer in a read-only session, the design is sound. That question, asked early, shapes the architecture; asked late, it becomes an incident review.
children.deep_text:
The exfiltration channel is the part that surprises people, because it does not require a tool named send_data. Any path from the agent to the outside world will do. An agent that renders markdown can be induced to emit an image reference whose URL embeds the conversation, and the fetch happens when the response is displayed. An agent that can browse can be told to visit a URL with data in the query string. An agent that writes to a shared document can leave data for someone else to collect. Enumerating outbound channels — including the indirect ones created by how your client renders output — is a necessary part of the threat model, and rendering is the one that gets missed.

Confused-deputy is the underlying pattern and naming it clarifies the fix. The agent holds authority the attacker does not, and the attack consists of persuading the agent to use that authority on the attacker's behalf. The remedy is not to make the agent more suspicious, since it will always be persuadable, but to reduce the authority it holds. An agent operating within one user's session, able to read only that user's documents, is limited by scope no matter what it is convinced to do. An agent with an ambient admin token is a single successful injection away from a breach, and no prompt hardening changes that.

Privilege separation extends the idea across the architecture, and it is where multi-agent design earns its keep. Split the system so that the component processing untrusted content holds no credentials, and the component holding credentials never sees raw untrusted text. A researcher subagent reads web pages and returns a structured, schema-validated summary; a coordinator with tool access consumes only that structured output. Injected instructions in the page are constrained to whatever can be smuggled through a narrow, validated schema, which is a dramatically smaller surface than free text. This is a real boundary because it is enforced by what each component can do, not by what it was asked to do.

Defence in depth still applies even though none of the individual layers is sufficient. Mark provenance in the context so untrusted content is clearly labelled and the model is instructed never to treat it as directive — imperfect, and it raises the bar. Screen inputs for known injection patterns — bypassable, and it stops opportunistic attempts. Screen outputs before rendering, particularly for URLs and links pointing at unexpected destinations. Rate-limit and anomaly-detect tool usage so a burst of unusual calls is caught. Log everything so an incident is investigable. The point is not that any of these prevents a determined attack; it is that the combination catches most real ones and makes the rest visible.

Two closing points. First, this is a live area with no complete solution, so architectural decisions should assume the model layer will remain fallible — designs that depend on injection being solved are designs that will fail. Second, the practical consequence is a clear guideline: an agent that reads untrusted content should not also hold the ability to take irreversible actions in the same session with the same privileges. Splitting those, whether across sessions, subagents, or a human confirmation step, is the single structural decision that prevents the large majority of realistic agent security incidents.

interview.question: Why can't prompt injection be fixed with better system prompts?
interview.answer: Because the model sees a single flat token sequence with no structural distinction between instructions it was given and text it merely read. Your system prompt, a retrieved document, and a fetched web page arrive in the same channel, so instruction-following applies to all of them. Stronger wording and delimiters raise the difficulty for casual attempts without changing the underlying situation. The boundary has to be enforced outside the model, by limiting what the executor is permitted to do.

interview.question: What is the exfiltration risk in an agent that has no tool for sending data?
interview.answer: Any outbound channel works, including ones created by rendering. If the client renders markdown, an injected instruction can produce an image reference whose URL encodes the conversation, and the fetch fires on display. A browsing tool can be pointed at a URL with data in the query string; a shared document becomes a dead drop. Threat modelling has to enumerate every path from the agent to the outside world, including client-side rendering, and allowlist outbound destinations.

interview.question: How do you design an agent that must read untrusted web content but also act on internal systems?
interview.answer: Separate the privileges. One component fetches and processes untrusted content and holds no credentials, returning a structured, schema-validated summary. A second component holds the credentials and consumes only that structured output, never the raw text. Injected instructions are then confined to what fits through a narrow validated schema instead of arriving as free text next to the tools. Add human confirmation for irreversible actions, and the realistic incident surface is close to eliminated.

children.deep_text:
It helps to be precise about the mechanics, because the word agent is used loosely enough to obscure what is actually happening. You send the model a list of tool definitions — name, description, and a JSON schema for the arguments — alongside the conversation. The model, having been trained on this format, may respond with a tool call instead of prose: a structured object naming a tool and supplying arguments. Your code receives that, validates it, decides whether to execute, executes it, and appends the result to the conversation as a tool-result message. Then you call the model again with the extended conversation. That is the entire loop. There is no daemon, no persistent process, no autonomy in any deep sense — just a while loop around a stateless function, where each iteration re-sends the whole history.

The units in this section follow the concerns that loop creates. The first covers the tool-calling mechanism itself and how tool design determines reliability — descriptions and schemas are prompt surface, and most tool-selection errors are specification errors rather than model errors. The second covers the loop: termination conditions, iteration budgets, error handling, and why a step that fails silently is worse than one that throws. The third covers architecture — when to use a fixed chain, when to use routing, when a genuine loop is warranted, and the multi-agent patterns and their real costs. The fourth covers the security surface, which is the part that turns an interesting demo into an incident.

The compounding-reliability point deserves to be internalised because it drives most architectural decisions. If each step succeeds independently with probability p, an n-step task succeeds with p to the n. At ninety-five percent per step, five steps give seventy-seven percent and twenty steps give thirty-six percent. There are exactly three responses: raise per-step reliability, reduce the number of steps, or add verification and recovery so failures do not propagate. Everything that works in production agent design is one of those three, and the second is usually the cheapest — a task decomposed into three deliberate tool calls is dramatically more reliable than the same task left to a model to figure out in fifteen.

The final framing to carry through: agentic is a spectrum, not a binary, and position on it should be chosen deliberately. At one end is a fixed pipeline where the model fills slots in a flow you wrote — predictable, testable, cheap, and limited to what you anticipated. At the other is an open loop with broad tool access that handles cases you never enumerated, at the cost of unpredictable latency, unpredictable spend, and a failure surface you cannot fully enumerate. Most production systems that work sit much closer to the fixed end than the demos suggest, and the discipline is to move toward autonomy only where the variety of the task genuinely demands it.

children.title: Evaluation
children.text:
Traditional software is verified by construction. You write a function, you assert what it returns, and if the assertion holds the function is correct — permanently, for that input. None of those properties survive contact with a language model. The same input yields different outputs across runs, there is usually no single correct output, and quality is a judgement rather than an equality check.

So correctness stops being a boolean and becomes a distribution you can only estimate by sampling. That is not a defect to be engineered away; it is the honest description of the system, and every practice in this section follows from accepting it. You cannot prove your assistant is good. You can measure how often it is good, on a fixed set of cases, and detect when that number moves.

The consequence is that evaluation is infrastructure, not a phase. Without it, every change — a prompt edit, a model upgrade, a chunking tweak, a temperature adjustment — is unverifiable. You ship, you check a few examples by hand, they look fine, and you have no idea whether you improved the median case while breaking a class of inputs you did not think to try. With it, the same change produces a number you can compare, and the whole workflow becomes empirical instead of superstitious.

The uncomfortable part is that this must be built before it is needed, and it always feels premature. Teams that skip it do not discover regressions; their users discover regressions, weeks later, and by then a dozen changes have landed and nobody can say which one caused it. A hundred labelled examples assembled early is worth more than any amount of prompt craftsmanship applied late.

children.title: Building Evaluation Datasets
children.text:
Everything in evaluation rests on the dataset, and a dataset assembled by engineers imagining user behaviour measures the wrong thing. Engineers write well-formed questions about functionality they know exists. Users write terse, ambiguous, misspelled questions, ask about things that do not exist, paste in walls of unformatted text, and switch topics mid-conversation. A system that scores well on the first population and has never been tested on the second is untested.

So real cases beat synthetic ones, and they are cheaper to obtain than teams expect. Support tickets, search logs, session transcripts, and the thumbs-down button are all sources of genuine inputs, complete with the messiness that makes them valuable. Fifty to a hundred of these, with an agreed notion of what a good response looks like, is enough to detect meaningful regressions — the useful threshold is far lower than the word dataset suggests.

Composition matters as much as size, because an average over an unrepresentative sample is a confident wrong number. The set needs the common cases that dominate traffic, the hard cases where the system is known to struggle, adversarial cases probing injection and misuse, and — the one most often missing — cases where the correct behaviour is to refuse or say it does not know. Systems never tested on unanswerable inputs almost always fail them, because nothing in the architecture distinguishes weak evidence from strong.

Treat the dataset as a living artefact under version control. Every production failure worth fixing becomes a case, so the set grows along the axis of things that have actually gone wrong, and the fix is verified by the same mechanism that will catch its regression later. That loop — failure to case to fix to permanent guard — is what makes quality accumulate rather than oscillate.
children.deep_text:
The most common structural mistake is a single undifferentiated set producing a single aggregate score. That number hides exactly the information you need: a change that improves the common path by three points while destroying performance on a rare but important category shows up as an improvement. Slicing by category, by difficulty, by input length, by user segment, and by whether the case is answerable turns one uninterpretable number into a profile where regressions are visible and localised. It costs nothing beyond labelling each case with its slice, and it changes what you can conclude.

Defining expected output is the part that requires the most thought, because for open-ended tasks there is no single right answer to store. Storing one and scoring by similarity to it is a well-known failure mode — it rewards imitation of an arbitrary phrasing rather than quality. The alternatives that work are criteria rather than answers. Store the facts that must appear, the claims that must not, the format that must hold, and the constraints that must be respected, then grade against those. This shifts effort from writing model answers to articulating what makes an answer good, which is harder, more useful, and directly reusable as the rubric for a model grader.

Synthetic data has a legitimate role with clear limits. It is good for expanding coverage of variations once you have real seeds — paraphrasing a real question ten ways to test robustness, generating edge cases within a known category, producing volume for a category where real examples are scarce. It is bad as a foundation, because generated cases carry the generating model's assumptions about what questions look like, which is precisely the bias you built the dataset to escape. The reasonable pattern is real cases as the backbone with synthetic expansion around them, never the reverse.

Contamination and staleness deserve explicit management. If your evaluation cases appear in public repositories or documentation, future models may have trained on them, and your scores become uninterpretable — keep a private held-out set. Separately, a dataset frozen at launch measures a distribution of usage that no longer exists, since the product changed and the users changed with it. Periodically resampling from recent production traffic keeps the set aligned with reality; without that, the score stays high while satisfaction falls, and the two numbers stop being related.

Finally, be deliberate about the split between the set you iterate against and the set you trust. Tuning prompts against a fixed set overfits to it — after twenty iterations, improvements on that set stop generalising because you have effectively been optimising against it by hand. Keep a held-out set that is evaluated rarely and never used to guide changes. When the development score improves and the held-out score does not, you have learned that the last several changes were fitting noise, which is a genuinely useful and otherwise invisible signal.

interview.question: Why are engineer-written test cases insufficient for evaluating an LLM product?
interview.answer: Because engineers write well-formed questions about features they know exist, and real users do not. Actual traffic contains terse, ambiguous, misspelled queries, questions about things the system does not cover, pasted unformatted text, and mid-conversation topic switches. A system evaluated only on the clean distribution has never been tested on the one it will face. Real cases from tickets, logs, and negative feedback carry that messiness for free, which is exactly what makes them valuable.

interview.question: Why is a single aggregate evaluation score dangerous?
interview.answer: Because it averages away the failures that matter. A change can lift the common case slightly while badly regressing a rare but important category, and the aggregate reports an improvement. Slicing by category, difficulty, input length, user segment, and answerability makes such regressions visible and tells you where they are. The labelling cost is trivial and it is the difference between a number you can act on and a number you can only watch.

interview.question: Your evaluation score keeps rising but users are not happier. What are the likely explanations?
interview.answer: Overfitting to the development set is the first — after many iterations of tuning against fixed cases, gains stop generalising, which a rarely-touched held-out set would reveal. The second is staleness: a set built at launch measures a usage distribution that has since changed, so the score describes an obsolete product. The third is metric mismatch, where the grader rewards something like verbosity or surface similarity to a reference rather than what users value. All three are diagnosed by checking against fresh production traffic and human review.

children.title: Metrics and Graders
children.text:
A grader is a function from output to score, and choosing one means deciding what quality means concretely enough to compute. The choices form a ladder from cheap and narrow to expensive and faithful, and the practical answer is almost always several rungs at once rather than one.

Exact match and its relatives work where a single correct answer exists — classification, extraction, routing, anything with a closed label set. They are deterministic, free, and unambiguous, and they cover far more of a real system than people assume once you look for the sub-tasks inside it rather than judging only the final prose.

Reference-overlap metrics like ROUGE and BLEU score similarity to a written answer. They are cheap and correlate weakly with quality for open-ended text, because a response can share most of its vocabulary with the reference and be wrong, or share almost none and be excellent. They are best treated as a coarse regression tripwire, not as a measure of goodness.

Programmatic property checks are the underrated rung. Rather than asking whether the output is good, assert specific verifiable properties: it parses as valid JSON against the schema, the generated code compiles and passes its tests, every citation resolves to a real retrieved chunk, no forbidden term appears, the length is within bounds. These are deterministic, fast enough to run on every request in production, and they catch a large share of real failures for almost no cost.

Above them sit model-based graders, which handle the genuinely subjective criteria — is this helpful, is it grounded, does it follow the rubric — at a scale humans cannot match, with biases that make them a tool requiring calibration rather than a source of truth.
children.deep_text:
The productive move when facing an apparently unmeasurable task is decomposition. Is this a good answer resists scoring, but it usually factors into components that do not. Does it address the question asked. Is every factual claim supported by the provided context. Does it follow the required format. Does it avoid the prohibited topics. Is it within the length target. Several of those are programmatic; the remainder are narrow enough that a model grader can be reliable about them. A profile of five component scores is also far more actionable than one holistic number, because a drop points at what broke.

Grading with reference to retrieved context is the highest-value model-based check in RAG systems and works best when framed decompositionally. Split the answer into atomic claims, then ask a grader, given only the retrieved passages, whether each claim is supported, contradicted, or unaddressed. This is close to natural-language inference, a task models handle well, and it yields per-claim verdicts you can inspect rather than a drifting holistic score. It also localises the failure to a specific sentence, which is what makes it actionable.

Statistical discipline is routinely skipped and routinely causes false conclusions. With a hundred cases, a two-point difference in score is noise, and treating it as a result leads teams to ship changes that did nothing and revert changes that helped. Report confidence intervals, or at minimum know roughly how large a difference the sample size can detect. Non-determinism compounds this: the same prompt on the same case can score differently across runs, so a fair comparison either fixes the seed and temperature where the provider allows it, or samples multiple generations per case and compares distributions. A single run of each variant is not evidence.

Cost and latency belong in the evaluation alongside quality, because they are the constraints under which quality is actually chosen. A change that improves accuracy by one point while doubling per-request cost is a business decision, not an engineering win, and presenting quality without the accompanying cost and latency numbers hides that decision. Reporting all three together makes the trade explicit and lets whoever owns the budget participate in it.

The final and most important property of a grader is that it should be hard to game. Any metric under optimisation pressure will be optimised, including in directions you did not intend. Graders that reward length produce padding. Graders that reward confident tone produce overconfidence. Graders that reward keyword presence produce keyword stuffing. Before adopting a metric, it is worth asking what the worst output that scores highly looks like — if that output is bad, the metric will eventually produce it, because the iteration loop is a search process and it will find whatever the metric actually rewards rather than what you meant.

interview.question: Why is similarity to a reference answer a poor metric for open-ended generation?
interview.answer: Because it measures surface overlap rather than quality. Two answers can share most of their vocabulary while one is factually wrong, and an excellent answer can phrase things entirely differently from the reference and score badly. It also implies the reference is the ideal, which for open-ended tasks it usually is not — it is one acceptable answer among many. It has some use as a coarse tripwire for gross regressions, but it should not be the basis for deciding whether a change helped.

interview.question: How would you make 'is this a good answer' measurable?
interview.answer: Decompose it. Split the question into components that can each be checked: does it address what was asked, is every claim supported by the provided context, does it satisfy the format, does it avoid prohibited content, is it within length. Several become deterministic programmatic checks, and the rest are narrow enough for a reliable model grader. The resulting profile is also more actionable than a single number, because a drop identifies which property broke.

interview.question: You run an evaluation twice on the same prompt and get different scores. How do you compare two variants fairly?
interview.answer: Treat the score as a sample from a distribution rather than a value. Fix seed and temperature where the provider supports it, or sample multiple generations per case and compare distributions rather than single runs. Report a confidence interval, because on a hundred cases a two-point difference is usually noise and acting on it means shipping changes that did nothing. Knowing the smallest difference your sample size can actually detect prevents most false conclusions.

children.title: LLM as Judge
children.text:
Using a model to grade another model's output is the technique that makes subjective evaluation practical, because it is the only method that scales to thousands of cases and still handles criteria like helpfulness, tone, and groundedness. Agreement with careful human raters is genuinely usable when the setup is careful — and the setup is where nearly all the difficulty lives.

The biases are documented and consistent enough to design around. Judges favour longer responses over shorter ones of equal quality. They favour the first option presented in a pairwise comparison. They favour outputs from the model family they belong to. They cluster their scores in the middle of a numeric range and rarely use the extremes. None of these is a reason to avoid the technique; each is a reason to construct the task so the bias cannot express itself.

The construction that works follows from that. Prefer pairwise comparison over absolute scoring, since which of these is better is a far easier judgement than rate this seven out of ten, and randomise the order of the pair to cancel position bias. Give a rubric with explicit criteria and concrete examples of each grade rather than an abstract scale. Ask for reasoning before the verdict, since the judgement then follows an articulated argument rather than being rationalised afterwards. Use a coarse scale with named levels, because a model does not meaningfully distinguish a six from a seven.

The non-negotiable step is calibration. Have humans grade a sample, measure agreement with the judge, and only then trust the judge at scale — and repeat it periodically, especially after changing the judge model or the rubric. An uncalibrated judge is an unfalsifiable opinion generator, and a system tuned against one optimises for whatever that judge happens to reward.
children.deep_text:
It is worth understanding why the technique works at all, because that explains where it stops working. Recognition is easier than generation, in models much as in people. Judging whether an answer is grounded in a passage is closer to a comparison and classification task than the open-ended synthesis that produced the answer, so a judge can reliably evaluate output it could not reliably have produced. This is also the boundary: a judge cannot assess correctness in a domain where it lacks the knowledge. Asking a general model to verify specialised clinical or legal claims yields confident, worthless verdicts. Where the judge lacks the knowledge, it must be given it — the retrieved passages, the documentation, the test results — so the task becomes verification against provided evidence rather than recall.

Position bias in pairwise comparison is large enough to invalidate results if ignored. The standard mitigation is to run each comparison twice with the order swapped and count only the cases where the verdict is consistent; inconsistent pairs are genuine ties and should be recorded as such rather than resolved arbitrarily. This doubles the cost and is the difference between a measurement and an artefact. The frequency of inconsistency is itself a useful diagnostic — a high rate means your rubric is not discriminating and needs sharper criteria.

Length bias interacts badly with the iteration loop, which is what makes it the most consequential of the biases. If the judge prefers longer answers, prompt iteration guided by that judge will steadily produce longer answers, and the score will rise while the product gets more verbose and less useful. Two defences are cheap: track output length alongside score so the correlation is visible, and state explicitly in the rubric that conciseness is a virtue and unnecessary length should be penalised. Without them the metric silently rewards padding and the loop obliges.

Self-preference is the reason to be careful about judge selection. A model tends to rate outputs from its own family more highly, which makes a same-family judge inappropriate for choosing between vendors. Using a different family, or an ensemble of judges from different families, removes the obvious conflict. For comparing prompt variants within a single model the concern is much smaller, since both candidates come from the same generator.

Two practices make judges trustworthy over time. First, keep a small human-graded gold set and re-run the judge against it whenever anything changes, treating agreement as a health metric for the judge itself — judges drift when the underlying model updates, and a drifted judge silently changes the meaning of every score you have. Second, log the judge's reasoning, not just its verdict. Reading twenty explanations reveals whether the judge is applying the rubric or has latched onto a superficial cue, and it is by far the fastest way to find that your evaluation has been measuring something other than what you intended.

interview.question: Why is pairwise comparison generally better than absolute scoring for an LLM judge?
interview.answer: Because relative judgement is an easier and more stable task than mapping quality onto an absolute scale. Judges cluster absolute scores in the middle of a range and drift in their interpretation of what a seven means, so the same output can score differently across runs and rubric versions. Which of these two is better is more consistent and more sensitive to real differences. The cost is that it requires order randomisation to cancel position bias, ideally by running both orders and keeping only consistent verdicts.

interview.question: Your judge scores keep improving as you iterate on prompts, but the answers feel worse. What is likely happening?
interview.answer: Length bias combined with the optimisation loop. Judges systematically prefer longer responses, so iterating against that judge steadily selects for verbosity and the score rises while usefulness falls. The diagnostics are to track output length alongside score and look for correlation, and to read the judge's stated reasoning to see whether it is applying the rubric or rewarding thoroughness-as-length. The fix is an explicit conciseness criterion in the rubric plus a length check as a separate reported metric.

interview.question: How do you know whether to trust an LLM judge at all?
interview.answer: By calibrating it against humans. Have people grade a sample of the same cases, measure agreement, and only scale up if agreement is acceptable for the decision you are making. Re-run that check periodically and whenever the judge model, its version, or the rubric changes, since judges drift and a drifted judge silently redefines every historical score. Without calibration the judge is an unfalsifiable opinion, and tuning against it optimises for whatever it happens to reward.

children.title: Evaluation in Practice
children.text:
Evaluation only pays off when it runs automatically. A suite that requires someone to remember to invoke it is a suite that stops running within a month, and the point is precisely to catch the change nobody thought was risky. Wiring it into continuous integration on every change to prompts, retrieval configuration, tool definitions, or model version is what converts it from an artefact into a guard.

Gate on regressions rather than on absolute thresholds. An absolute bar is either so low it never fires or so high it blocks legitimate work, whereas a rule that flags any statistically meaningful drop from the current baseline directly targets what you care about. Slice-level gates matter more than the aggregate, since a change that trades a rare category for the common one should surface as a decision rather than pass as an improvement.

Offline evaluation is necessary and never sufficient, because your dataset is a snapshot of the inputs you knew about. Production carries a different distribution and it moves. So the offline suite is paired with online signals — thumbs, regeneration rate, conversation abandonment, escalation to a human, task completion — which are noisy individually and reliable in aggregate, and which cover the cases you never imagined.

The loop that closes the two is what makes quality accumulate. A production failure is triaged, becomes a dataset case, is fixed, and is thereafter permanently guarded by the suite that caught nothing before. Over months the dataset comes to encode everything that has ever gone wrong, and the system stops regressing along axes it has already been fixed on. That ratchet is the actual payoff of the whole section.
children.deep_text:
Cost and runtime shape how the suite is used, and ignoring that produces a suite people route around. A thousand cases graded by a strong judge with multiple samples each is slow enough and expensive enough that nobody runs it on a pull request. The standard resolution is tiering. A fast tier of deterministic programmatic checks and a few dozen critical cases runs on every commit in a minute or two. A full tier with model grading across the whole dataset runs before release or nightly. A deep tier including human review runs on major changes. Each tier is trusted only for what it can catch, and the fast one exists to be cheap enough that nobody skips it.

Model version upgrades are the scenario the whole apparatus exists for, and they are consistently underestimated. A new model version can improve average quality while changing behaviour in ways that break your system: different formatting habits that defeat a parser, different verbosity that overflows a context budget, different refusal boundaries that decline requests the old version handled, different tool-calling tendencies that alter agent trajectories. Running the full suite against the candidate before switching is the only way to see this, and the slice-level view is essential because the aggregate will often look fine while a specific category collapses. Keeping the ability to pin and roll back a model version is part of the same discipline.

A/B testing is the arbiter when offline and online signals disagree, and they will. Offline evaluation measures a proxy on a fixed set; a live experiment measures what actually happens to real users.
