When a change looks better offline and worse online, the online result is the truth and the offline metric has been shown to be miscalibrated — which is valuable information about the metric. Treat that as a signal to fix the evaluation, not to dismiss the experiment.

Instrumentation is the precondition for all of it, and it should be in place before the first evaluation is written. Log inputs, retrieved context identifiers, the assembled prompt or a hash of it, the model and version, sampling parameters, the raw output, token counts, latency, and any user feedback signal. That record is what allows a production failure to be turned into a reproducible case, and without it triage becomes speculation. Retention policy and PII handling need deciding at the same time, since the log contains user content by construction.

The organisational point is the one that determines whether any of this survives. Evaluation infrastructure is usually built by whoever cares most and then decays once that person moves on, because it produces no visible feature. It stays alive when the numbers are visible to the team on a dashboard, when the gate genuinely blocks merges, and when adding a case for every production failure is a normal expectation rather than a favour. The technical work here is modest; making it durable is the harder problem, and it is worth naming as such rather than assuming good intentions will carry it.

interview.question: Why gate on regression from a baseline rather than on an absolute quality threshold?
interview.answer: Because an absolute threshold is either set low enough that it never fires or high enough that it blocks legitimate work, and neither tells you what you want to know. What matters is whether this change made things worse. A rule that flags a statistically meaningful drop from the current baseline targets that directly, and applying it per slice rather than only to the aggregate catches changes that trade a rare category for the common one — which should be a deliberate decision, not a silent pass.

interview.question: A model version upgrade improves your average score. Why is that not sufficient to ship it?
interview.answer: Because averages hide behavioural changes that break integrations. A new version can format differently and defeat a parser, be more verbose and overflow a context budget, refuse a category the old one handled, or call tools with different frequency and change agent trajectories. Slice-level comparison is what exposes these, and the ability to pin and roll back the version is what makes the upgrade safe to attempt at all.

interview.question: Offline evaluation says a change is better; the live A/B test says it is worse. Which do you believe?
interview.answer: The A/B test, because it measures real users rather than a proxy on a fixed set. The disagreement is also a finding in its own right: it means the offline metric is miscalibrated against what users actually value, so the response is to investigate why — often length bias in a judge, a stale dataset, or a rubric rewarding the wrong property — and fix the evaluation. Dismissing the experiment to defend the metric is exactly backwards.

children.deep_text:
The core difficulty is that most interesting outputs have no reference answer. Classification has one and can be scored with accuracy. Summarisation, explanation, code generation, and conversation have a space of acceptable outputs and a space of unacceptable ones, with the boundary defined by criteria that are easy to recognise and hard to state. Evaluation methodology for these systems is largely the craft of converting recognisable quality into something measurable, and every available method is a different trade between fidelity and cost.

There are three, and they are complementary rather than ranked. Programmatic checks are cheap, deterministic, and only cover properties expressible in code — does it parse, does it compile, does it contain the required identifier, is it under the length limit, does every citation resolve. Model-based grading covers subjective criteria at scale with acceptable and biased agreement with humans. Human review is the ground truth that calibrates the other two and does not scale. A working system uses all three: programmatic checks on every request, model grading on every change, human review on a sample to keep the graders honest.

The units here follow that structure. The first covers building datasets, which is the part that determines whether anything downstream is meaningful — where cases come from, why real failures beat imagined ones, and how to keep the set from going stale. The second covers metrics and graders, from exact-match through rubric-based scoring, and what each actually measures. The third covers LLM-as-judge specifically, because it is now the workhorse of practical evaluation and it has documented, exploitable biases that must be designed around. The fourth covers running evaluation as a process — regression gates, online metrics, and the loop from production failure back into the dataset.

One framing to carry through: the goal is not a high score. It is a fast, trustworthy signal about whether a change helped. A metric that is easy to game, or that correlates weakly with what users care about, actively misleads — it will reward changes that raise the number and degrade the product. The question to ask about any evaluation is not whether it is rigorous but whether a change that improves it reliably improves the experience of the person using the system.

children.title: Serving, Cost and Reliability
children.text:
Inference is not a normal API call and the differences all trace to one mechanical fact: output is generated one token at a time, each token requiring a full forward pass that depends on every token before it. Nothing about that is parallelisable within a single response. So latency is roughly proportional to output length, and the single most effective way to make a response faster is to make it shorter.

That decomposition gives you the two numbers that matter and they behave differently. Time to first token covers reading the input, which the hardware processes in parallel and which is therefore fast and only weakly dependent on prompt length. Time between subsequent tokens is fixed by the serial generation loop. A response of five hundred tokens simply cannot arrive faster than five hundred sequential passes allow, regardless of how much hardware you have.

Streaming follows directly and is the highest-leverage latency work available, because it changes perceived latency without changing the computation at all. Deliver tokens as they are produced and the user begins reading after a few hundred milliseconds instead of waiting for the whole response. The total time is identical; the experience is not remotely.

Cost has the same structure. You pay per token in both directions, so cost per request is set by architectural choices — how much context you assemble, how many chunks you retrieve, how many agent iterations you allow, how verbose the output is — rather than by anything you can negotiate later. Caching, model tiering, and context discipline are the levers, and they are levers on the design, which is why unit economics need to be understood while the design is still soft.

children.title: Latency and Streaming
children.text:
Latency in an LLM system decomposes into pieces with very different tractability, and knowing which is which prevents most wasted optimisation. Time to first token is the sum of network round trip, queueing at the provider, and prefill over your prompt. Generation time is the token count multiplied by the per-token interval, and that interval is set by the model and the serving stack rather than by anything in your control.

The consequence is blunt: output length is the dominant lever. Halving a response halves the generation time, and no other single change comes close. Which means prompt instructions that constrain length, output schemas that do not invite elaboration, and resisting the temptation to ask for reasoning you will not use are latency work, even though they look like prompt engineering.

Streaming is the highest-return change available because it decouples perceived latency from total latency. The first token arriving in three hundred milliseconds feels responsive even if the full response takes eight seconds, whereas the same response delivered whole feels broken. The costs are real but manageable: you cannot validate output you have already displayed, so schema-constrained or moderated responses either stream with post-hoc correction or do not stream at all, and error handling mid-stream needs an explicit design since the status code was already sent.

Beyond that, the reliable techniques are structural. Overlap independent work — start retrieval while the user is still typing, run independent tool calls concurrently, prefetch what you can predict. Route easy requests to a smaller, faster model. And be explicit about latency budgets per stage, because a pipeline of a retrieval, a rerank, and two model calls has a floor that no amount of tuning removes, and the only real fix is removing a stage.
children.deep_text:
Tail latency deserves more attention than the average, because it determines whether the system feels dependable. Inference latency distributions have long tails driven by queueing under load, variable output length, and occasional slow requests, so a p50 of two seconds can sit alongside a p99 of thirty. Users experience the tail — it is the request they remember — and a system optimised only for the median can feel unreliable while its dashboard looks healthy. Measure and report percentiles, and set timeouts against the tail rather than the mean.

Streaming introduces a class of design problems that are easy to overlook until they bite. Once a token is on the user's screen you cannot retract it, so any validation that would have rejected the response must now be handled visibly. If the output must conform to a schema, you either buffer and lose the latency benefit, or stream and repair, or stream only the natural-language portion while buffering the structured part. If a content filter fires mid-generation you must stop and replace visibly rather than silently. And a stream that fails halfway leaves the client holding a partial response with the HTTP status long since sent, which means errors have to be signalled in-band as part of the event protocol. None of these is difficult, but all of them need designing rather than discovering.

Perceived latency responds to things that are not latency at all, and that lever is cheap. Showing what the system is doing — retrieving sources, calling a tool, drafting — converts dead time into progress and measurably increases tolerance for waiting. Streaming intermediate agent steps rather than only the final answer does the same for long-running tasks. Rendering incrementally as markdown resolves keeps the surface feeling live. These do not make anything faster, and they change the experience more than a second of real improvement typically would.

The interaction between latency and quality is a genuine trade to make deliberately rather than a problem to solve. Chain-of-thought reasoning improves accuracy on hard problems and multiplies output tokens, hence latency and cost. Retrieval improves grounding and adds a round trip. Reranking improves precision and adds a model call. Reflection improves quality on some tasks and doubles everything. Each is justified for hard requests and wasteful for easy ones, which is the argument for routing: classify the request cheaply, then spend the expensive machinery only where it pays. A router that sends eighty percent of traffic down a fast path is usually a larger win than any optimisation of the slow path.

Finally, place caching where it can eliminate work entirely rather than merely accelerate it. Prompt caching cuts prefill cost for a shared prefix and is nearly free to adopt if your prompt is structured with stable content first. A semantic cache that recognises a near-duplicate query and returns a stored answer removes the model call altogether, which is the only intervention that takes latency to near zero — at the risk of returning a stale or subtly mismatched answer, which is why it suits stable factual domains and suits conversational, personalised, or fast-changing content badly.

interview.question: Why does prompt length affect latency much less than response length?
interview.answer: Because the two phases work differently. Prefill processes all input tokens in parallel in a single pass, so it is compute-efficient and grows sub-proportionally with prompt size. Decode generates one token per forward pass, each pass reading the whole model from memory, and those passes are strictly sequential because each token depends on the last. A long prompt with a short answer is cheap in latency; a short prompt with a long answer is not, which makes output length the dominant lever.

interview.question: What do you lose by streaming, and how do you handle it?
interview.answer: You lose the ability to validate before displaying. Schema violations, content-filter triggers, and mid-stream failures all occur after output is visible and after the status code was sent. The handling options are to buffer the structured portion while streaming the prose, to stream and visibly correct or truncate, and to signal errors in-band through the event protocol rather than relying on HTTP status. None is hard, but each has to be designed rather than discovered in production.

interview.question: Your p50 latency is fine but users complain the product feels slow. Where do you look?
interview.answer: The tail. Inference latency distributions are long-tailed because of queueing under load and variable output length, so a healthy median can coexist with a p99 that is an order of magnitude worse, and users remember the slow request. I would report percentiles rather than averages, set timeouts against the tail, and check whether long outputs are driving it. Alongside that, progress indication and streaming intermediate steps improve tolerance substantially without changing any real number.

children.title: Caching and Cost Control
children.text:
Cost per request is determined at design time, because you pay per token and the token count is a consequence of architecture. Context assembly, retrieved chunk count, agent iterations, and output verbosity each multiply into the bill, and none of them is adjustable after the fact without changing the system. The first step is therefore to compute cost per request explicitly and multiply by expected volume, before the design hardens.

Prompt caching is the cheapest large win and it has one structural requirement: the cached portion must be a stable prefix. Providers cache the processed state of a prompt's leading tokens, so identical prefixes across requests skip prefill and are billed at a steep discount. This makes prompt ordering an economic decision — system instructions, tool definitions, and few-shot examples belong at the front, and anything that varies per request belongs at the end. Inserting a timestamp near the top of an otherwise stable prompt invalidates the cache on every call and is a genuinely common and expensive mistake.

Model tiering is the other structural lever. Capability and price differ by an order of magnitude across a provider's range, and most traffic does not need the top of the range. Classifying, extracting, routing, and summarising short text are handled well by small models; the expensive one earns its cost on hard reasoning. Routing on request complexity, or cascading from cheap to expensive when the cheap answer fails a check, typically cuts cost far more than token-level tuning.

Beyond those, the reliable savings are the boring ones. Retrieve fewer, better chunks after reranking rather than many mediocre ones. Cap agent iterations. Constrain output length. Summarise stale conversation history instead of resending it. Each is a small change and they compound, because every one of them reduces tokens on every subsequent request in the same session.
children.deep_text:
Semantic caching is the intervention with the largest upside and the sharpest risk, so it needs scoping rather than a yes or no. Embedding an incoming query and returning a stored response when a previous query is sufficiently close eliminates the model call entirely — not accelerates it, eliminates it — which is unmatched for both cost and latency. The risk is that similarity is not equivalence. How do I cancel my subscription and how do I cancel my subscription without a fee are close in embedding space and have different answers, and a threshold loose enough to be useful will sometimes return the wrong one. Semantic caching therefore fits stable factual domains with high query repetition — documentation and support FAQs — and fits personalised, conversational, or fast-changing content badly. Where it is used, the threshold must be tuned against real query pairs, entries must expire when underlying content changes, and any personalisation or tenant identity must be part of the cache key or the cache becomes a data-leak channel.

Where the money actually goes is usually surprising when measured, and measuring it per feature rather than in aggregate is what makes it actionable. Common findings: an agent loop consuming ten times the tokens of a single-turn feature because it re-sends its history each iteration; a RAG path retrieving twenty chunks when five reranked chunks score better; a system prompt bloated with accumulated instructions that is paid for on every single request; a conversation feature with no history truncation where long sessions cost hundreds of times what short ones do. Instrumenting token counts by feature and by user, and looking at the distribution rather than the mean, is generally a day of work that finds a large saving.

Fine-tuning belongs in the cost conversation because it is often framed as a quality technique when its clearest economic case is cost. A fine-tuned small model can match a large model's quality on a narrow task while costing a fraction per request and running faster. The economics turn on volume: the training cost and the ongoing maintenance burden are fixed, so at low volume prompting a large model is cheaper, and at high volume on a stable task fine-tuning wins decisively. The break-even is worth computing rather than assuming, and the maintenance cost — retraining when the task drifts or a better base model appears — is the part usually omitted from the estimate.

Batch processing deserves mention because it is free money for the workloads it suits. Providers offer substantial discounts for asynchronous batch jobs with relaxed latency guarantees, since these fill capacity troughs. Anything not user-facing — bulk classification, embedding a corpus, generating summaries overnight, running an evaluation suite — should be on the batch path. Teams routinely pay interactive rates for offline work simply because the code was written against the synchronous endpoint first.

Finally, treat spend as an operational metric with the same seriousness as error rate. Per-request and per-user cost limits, alerts on anomalous spend, and hard caps in agent loops are guardrails against both bugs and abuse. A retry loop that does not terminate, or a single user driving unbounded requests, can produce a very large bill very quickly, and the difference between a minor incident and a serious one is usually whether a cap was in place before it happened rather than any detection after.

interview.question: How does prompt caching change how you structure a prompt?
interview.answer: It makes ordering economically significant. Providers cache the processed state of a leading prefix, so anything stable — system instructions, tool definitions, few-shot examples, static context — belongs at the front, and per-request content belongs at the end. The common expensive mistake is putting something variable like a timestamp or a session id near the top, which invalidates the cache on every request and silently forfeits the discount while the prompt looks perfectly reasonable.

interview.question: When is semantic caching a good idea, and when is it dangerous?
interview.answer: It suits stable factual domains with high query repetition, like documentation or support FAQs, where near-duplicate questions genuinely have the same answer and skipping the model call entirely is a large win. It is dangerous where similarity does not imply equivalence — how to cancel and how to cancel without a fee sit close in embedding space with different answers — and in personalised or conversational contexts, where it also becomes a data-leak channel unless user or tenant identity is part of the cache key.

interview.question: Cost per request is too high. Where do you look before tuning prompts?
interview.answer: At architecture, because that is what sets the token count. Measure tokens per feature and look for the structural offenders: an agent loop re-sending its history every iteration, retrieval passing twenty chunks where five reranked ones do better, an accumulated system prompt paid for on every call, conversations with no history truncation. Then apply the structural levers — model tiering so cheap requests use a cheap model, prompt caching on a stable prefix, batch pricing for anything not user-facing. Those dominate token-level editing.

children.title: Reliability and Failure Handling
children.text:
LLM APIs fail in ways that make some standard reliability patterns actively harmful. Requests are slow, so timeouts must be generous, which means a hung request occupies a connection for a long time. Requests are expensive, so a naive retry doubles cost as well as latency. Rate limits are enforced on tokens as well as requests, so a client well under its request quota can still be throttled by a few large prompts.

Timeouts need to be set against the tail of the distribution and against output length rather than picked as a round number. Streaming complicates this usefully: an idle timeout between tokens is a better signal of a stuck request than a total-duration timeout, because a long healthy response and a hung one look identical to a wall-clock limit but entirely different to a token-gap limit.

Retries need to distinguish failure types, and the distinction is what makes them safe. Rate limits and transient server errors merit retry with exponential backoff and jitter — without jitter, a fleet retrying in lockstep produces synchronised bursts that prolong the outage they are responding to. Invalid requests and content-policy refusals will fail identically forever and must not be retried. Timeouts are ambiguous, because the work may have completed and been billed, so retrying one is a cost decision as well as a correctness one.

Fallbacks are what keep the system available when the primary path is not. A secondary provider or a smaller model, a cached or precomputed response, or an honest degraded message all beat a spinner. The design constraint is that a fallback must be tested, since an untested fallback path is a second outage waiting for the first, and it is exercised for the first time at the worst moment.
children.deep_text:
Token-based rate limiting is the part that trips up teams accustomed to request-based quotas. Limits are typically expressed in both requests per minute and tokens per minute, and the token limit binds first for any application with substantial prompts. Client-side throttling therefore has to account for estimated tokens per request rather than counting requests, and a single large request can consume a meaningful fraction of a minute's budget. The practical approach is a token-aware limiter that estimates prompt size before sending, queues when the budget is exhausted, and applies backpressure to callers rather than letting requests fail. Priority tiers within that queue keep interactive requests ahead of background work, which is otherwise a common source of user-visible failures caused entirely by internal batch jobs.

Idempotency is subtler here than in ordinary APIs because generation is non-deterministic. Retrying a request does not produce the same output, so a retry after an ambiguous timeout can result in two different responses for one logical operation, and if the request had side effects — an agent that sent an email before the timeout — the effect may have occurred already. Where a provider supports idempotency keys, use them. Where the request drives tool execution, the tools themselves need idempotency, since the safety of the retry depends on the executor rather than the model.

Graceful degradation should be a designed ladder rather than an all-or-nothing switch. If reranking fails, serve the unreranked retrieval. If retrieval fails entirely, answer from the model's own knowledge with an explicit caveat, or decline. If the primary model is unavailable, fall back to a smaller one and mark the response accordingly. Each rung is worse than the one above and much better than an error page, and defining them in advance means the degraded behaviour is chosen rather than emergent.

Circuit breakers apply with the usual logic and an added cost dimension. When a provider is failing, continuing to send requests wastes money on calls that will fail and delays recovery by adding load. Breaking the circuit after a threshold of failures, serving fallbacks while open, and probing periodically before closing is standard and worth implementing per provider and per model, since a single model can be degraded while the rest of the provider is healthy.

Monitoring needs to cover a class of failure that has no error code. A model that starts returning malformed JSON, refusing legitimate requests, or producing much shorter answers than usual is failing while every request returns a successful status. The signals that catch this are behavioural: schema validation failure rate, refusal rate, output length distribution, retrieval score distribution, and empty or truncated response rate. Alerting on shifts in these catches silent degradation from a provider-side model update, which is the most common way a working system stops working without anyone changing anything.

interview.question: Why is a naive retry policy worse for LLM APIs than for ordinary services?
interview.answer: Because retries are expensive and slow rather than nearly free. A retry doubles token cost and adds seconds, and it may duplicate work that already completed and was billed if the original timed out after the server finished. It can also worsen the condition that caused the failure, since retrying into a rate limit consumes more of the same budget. Retries must be typed — backoff with jitter for rate limits and transient errors, no retry for invalid requests or policy refusals — and ambiguous timeouts treated as a deliberate cost decision.

interview.question: Your request rate is well under the limit but you are still being throttled. What is happening?
interview.answer: The token-per-minute limit is binding rather than the request limit. Rate limits are typically enforced on both, and for applications with large prompts the token budget is exhausted first, so a modest request rate with big contexts hits the ceiling. The fix is a token-aware client-side limiter that estimates prompt size before sending and queues against the token budget, with priority tiers so background jobs cannot starve interactive traffic.

interview.question: How do you detect a model degrading when every request still returns 200?
interview.answer: With behavioural metrics rather than error rates. Track schema validation failure rate, refusal rate, output length distribution, retrieval score distribution, and the rate of empty or truncated responses, then alert on distribution shifts. Silent degradation from a provider-side model update is the usual cause and it produces no errors at all — a parser starts failing more often or answers get shorter, and nothing in conventional monitoring notices. This is also where the offline evaluation suite earns its cost, run on a schedule against production configuration.

children.title: Safety, Abuse and Operations
children.text:
Exposing a model to the public creates an operational surface that has no analogue in a conventional API. The input is unstructured natural language, so it cannot be validated in the usual sense; the output is generated rather than selected, so it cannot be fully anticipated; and the component is expensive to run, so wasting its capacity is itself an attack.

Abuse takes predictable forms. There is cost abuse, where an attacker drives expensive requests to run up your bill or exhaust your rate limits. There is capability theft, where your product becomes a free proxy to a frontier model for someone else's purposes. And there is content abuse, where the system is manipulated into producing material you do not want associated with your product. The controls are ordinary — authentication, per-user quotas on tokens rather than requests, input length caps, anomaly detection — and they need to exist before launch rather than after the first bill.

Content safety works in layers because no single layer is sufficient. Provider-side filters catch the obvious cases. Your own input screening catches domain-specific misuse. System prompts establish scope and refusal behaviour, which shapes typical behaviour without being a security boundary. Output screening before display catches what got through. Each layer is porous and the combination is what makes the system defensible in practice.

The operational discipline that ties it together is logging with enough fidelity to investigate. When someone reports that the system said something it should not have, you need the input, the assembled context, the model and version, the sampling parameters, and the output — and you need it under a retention and privacy policy decided deliberately, because that log contains user content by construction.
children.deep_text:
Scope enforcement is the practical safety concern for most products, more than the dramatic misuse cases. A support assistant should decline to write poetry, give medical advice, or discuss competitors, not because those are dangerous but because they are off-brand, unbounded, and occasionally embarrassing when screenshotted. System prompts handle the ordinary cases and are trivially circumvented by anyone trying, which is the right way to think about them — they shape the typical interaction, and a determined user is a separate problem addressed by input classification and output screening. Deciding in advance which of the two you actually need is worth doing explicitly, because treating a system prompt as a security control is a category error that produces false confidence.

The right response to a jailbreak depends on who is doing it, and conflating the cases produces bad policy. A curious user probing boundaries is not a threat and should meet a graceful refusal. A user systematically attempting to extract training data, generate prohibited content at volume, or use your endpoint as a free proxy is an abuse case and belongs in rate limiting, account action, and anomaly detection rather than in prompt engineering. Trying to solve the second problem with better refusal instructions is the common mistake, and it fails because the model layer is not where the leverage is.

PII handling needs an explicit design because user input contains personal data whether or not you asked for it. Decisions to make deliberately: whether prompts are logged at all and for how long, whether PII is redacted before logging, whether user content is sent to third-party providers and what their retention terms are, whether it may be used for training, and how a deletion request propagates to logs, caches, and vector indexes. That last one is routinely overlooked — an embedding derived from a user's document sits in a vector index, and a deletion request has to reach it, which requires the index to carry the metadata linking vectors back to their subject. Retrofitting that is painful, and adding it at index time is nearly free.

Regulatory context increasingly requires disclosure and human recourse. Users should be told they are interacting with an AI system rather than discovering it. Consequential decisions need a human path, both because it is often legally required and because it is the honest response to a system that is right most of the time rather than always. Documenting intended use, known limitations, and evaluation results is becoming standard practice and is also useful internally, since writing down what the system is not for reliably surfaces disagreements that were previously implicit.

The closing operational point is that these systems change underneath you. The provider updates the model, the retrieval corpus grows, user behaviour shifts, and the same code produces different behaviour than it did last quarter. That makes ongoing measurement a requirement rather than a project phase — the evaluation suite running on a schedule against production configuration, behavioural metrics monitored for drift, a sample of real interactions reviewed by humans regularly, and a channel by which user reports become evaluation cases. A system nobody is measuring is not stable; it is drifting unobserved, and it will be the users who notice first.

interview.question: Why is a system prompt not a security control?
interview.answer: Because it is advisory text in the same channel as everything else the model reads, so it shapes typical behaviour and is circumvented by anyone deliberately trying. It is the right tool for scope and tone — keeping an assistant on topic for ordinary users — and the wrong tool for anything where a determined adversary is in the threat model. Real controls sit outside the model: input classification, output screening, rate limits, authentication, and restricting what the executor is permitted to do.

interview.question: What forms does abuse of a public LLM endpoint take?
interview.answer: Cost abuse, where an attacker drives expensive requests to run up the bill or exhaust rate limits; capability theft, where the endpoint is used as a free proxy to a frontier model for unrelated purposes; and content abuse, where the system is manipulated into producing material damaging to associate with the product. The controls are conventional — authentication, per-user token quotas rather than request quotas, input length caps, anomaly detection on usage patterns — and they need to exist before launch, since the first indication otherwise is the invoice.

interview.question: A user requests deletion of their data. What is easy to miss in an AI system?
interview.answer: The derived artefacts. Deleting the source document is straightforward; the embedding of that document in the vector index, the cached responses derived from it, and the prompt logs containing its content are all separate copies. Reaching them requires metadata at index time linking every vector and cache entry back to its subject, which is nearly free to add up front and painful to retrofit. Third-party retention also matters, since content sent to a provider is governed by their terms and needs to be part of the same policy.

children.deep_text:
The prefill and decode distinction is worth carrying because it explains most otherwise-puzzling performance behaviour. Prefill processes the entire input prompt in parallel — all positions at once — so it is compute-bound and remarkably efficient, and doubling the prompt length raises time to first token far less than proportionally. Decode generates one token per forward pass, and each pass must read the entire model's weights from memory to produce a single token, which makes it memory-bandwidth-bound and deeply inefficient per unit of work. That asymmetry has a direct engineering consequence: a large prompt producing a short answer is cheap in latency, and a small prompt producing a long answer is expensive. Engineers who assume a long prompt is the problem often optimise the wrong side.

Batching is how providers make decode economical and it explains a serving trade-off you will encounter whether you self-host or not. Because decode is bandwidth-bound, processing many sequences concurrently amortises the cost of reading the weights across all of them, raising throughput enormously at some cost to individual latency. Continuous batching, where new requests join a running batch as others finish, is the standard modern approach. If you are using a hosted API this is invisible but still governs your experience; if you are self-hosting it is the single most important thing to configure correctly.

The KV cache is the other structural artefact and it drives cost in conversations and agents. Attention at each step needs the key and value vectors for every preceding token, so they are cached rather than recomputed — which is what makes generation feasible and also means memory grows linearly with sequence length and with batch size. Long contexts consume serving memory, which limits batch size, which reduces throughput. This is why long-context requests are disproportionately expensive to serve, and it connects directly to the quadratic cost growth of agent loops and long chats discussed earlier.

The units here work through the consequences. Latency and streaming covers what can and cannot be made faster, and how to spend a latency budget. Caching and cost covers prompt caching, semantic caching, model tiering, and where the money actually goes. Reliability covers timeouts, retries, fallbacks, and rate limits, where the failure characteristics differ enough from ordinary services that standard patterns need adjusting. Security and abuse covers the operational surface — the boundary you inherit by accepting untrusted input into a component that generates text and may hold tools.

The framing worth keeping is that these are design decisions, not tuning parameters. You cannot retrofit acceptable cost per request onto a system that retrieves twenty chunks, runs a fifteen-step agent loop, and generates a thousand-token response, because the cost is the architecture. Knowing the per-request economics early is what keeps the architecture affordable rather than discovering at scale that it never was.

The clean way to see the shape of this field is to ask what remains unsolved once a capable model exists, because the answer is: nearly everything a product needs. A model, in isolation, is stateless, knowledge-frozen, sandboxed, unreliable in format, unbounded in cost, and indifferent to whether it is being manipulated. Each of those gaps is a section of this topic, and the sections are ordered so that each one supplies vocabulary the next one uses.

The first section establishes the substrate: what the model is as a computational object, what tokens and context windows actually are, why sampling makes outputs non-deterministic, and where the boundary sits between what the model does and what you must do. Skipping it is the single most common reason engineers develop superstitions about prompting — they attribute to intent what is really an artefact of tokenisation, sampling, or position in the context.

The second section is context engineering: the prompt as the model's entire observable universe for a given call. Because the model has no memory and no access to your systems, every fact it uses must appear in the context window, and the discipline is about deciding what earns a place there. This covers instruction design, few-shot demonstration, structured output, and how conversational memory is reconstructed on every single turn rather than stored.

The third section is retrieval. Context is finite and your corpus is not, so you need a mechanism that selects the small relevant slice at query time. That mechanism is built from embeddings, vector indexes, chunking decisions, and hybrid ranking — and it fails in ways that have nothing to do with the model, which is why retrieval quality is measured separately from answer quality.

The fourth section is agents and tool use, where the model stops producing text and starts causing effects. The moment a model's output triggers an API call, three new problems arrive at once: the loop may not terminate, individual steps compound their error rates multiplicatively, and the blast radius of a mistake is no longer a bad paragraph. Agent design is mostly the discipline of constraining all three.

The fifth section is evaluation, which is where systems become trustworthy or do not. Non-determinism and subjective quality make traditional testing insufficient, so you build datasets, define graders, accept the biases of LLM-as-judge, and run regression checks against every prompt and model change. Teams that skip this do not find out their system degraded; they find out from users.

The sixth section is production: latency, throughput, caching, cost per request, streaming, failure handling, and the security surface created by putting untrusted text in front of a component with tools. This is the part that resembles conventional systems engineering most, and it is where the economics of an AI product are actually decided.

Read in order. Retrieval assumes context engineering, agents assume both, evaluation assumes there is a system worth measuring, and production assumes the system works before you optimise it.
